title: Shit For Brains: A TBI Guide
author: Joseph Lewis

sections.h: A note from Joe and Alisha
p: November 2026. This book is a guide to living with a brain injury, and as it says at the start, it is not medical advice. Near the end, Joe calls Aetheria "frequency healing" and our music "healing frequency songs". We wrote it before we settled a rule our apps now follow: we don't say a sound heals or cures. Read those lines as where we were then. The book is as printed.
SHIT FOR BRAINS
A TBI Guide
Joseph Lewis
With contributions from Alisha Lewis
This book is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. Please consult qualified healthcare providers for medical decisions.

sections.h: Author's Note: Welcome to the Club
p: (Nobody Wanted to Join) ••• If you're holding this book, something bad probably happened. Maybe it happened to you. Maybe it happened to someone you love. Either way, welcome to the club nobody wanted to join. Membership is permanent, the benefits suck, and there's no option to cancel your subscription. But here's what they don't tell you at orientation: it gets easier. Not better, necessarily—I'm not going to blow sunshine up your ass and tell you it all works out and you'll be back to normal in no time. "Normal" left the building. "Normal" packed its bags, flipped you off, and moved to a country without an extradition treaty. But easier? Yeah. That happens. Eventually. I'm going to tell you how. ••• Who the Hell Am I? My name is Joe Lewis. Retired Staff Sergeant Lewis, if we're being formal—United States Air Force, Explosive Ordnance Disposal technician. Seven years. One deployment to Kandahar, Afghanistan, 2010-2011. I used to disarm bombs for a living. Funny thing is, it wasn't a bomb that got me. In October 2013, I was driving to work on a dirt road. What happened next, I don't remember. I've been told I flipped my car—a blue Scion tC—several times. I was ejected from the vehicle. They found me unconscious in a field. I was clinically dead. They life-flighted me to the trauma hospital in Boise. I had a shattered C-spine, broken back, broken ankle, broken ribs, collapsed lungs, and a severe traumatic brain injury. My frontal lobe took the worst of it, which—fun fact—is the part of your brain that controls impulse control, emotional regulation, and your ability to not say stupid shit in public. We'll get to that. The doctors told my wife they didn't know if I'd ever wake up. And if I did, they didn't know who I'd be when I opened my eyes. Spoiler alert: I woke up. But they were right about that second part.

The Part Where I Died (Briefly) Here's something I don't tell a lot of people, but I figure if you're reading a book called "Shit For Brains," you can probably handle it. I had a near-death experience. While my body was lying in that field, I went somewhere else. I saw golden clouds—I know how that sounds, but that's what they were—and a door made of light. And standing in front of that door was my best friend. He'd died a year earlier. Motorcycle accident. He looked at me and said, "You don't belong here." I probably said something stupid back. That's kind of my thing. Then he said, "You have a big job to do." And he pushed me. I fell, and I woke up naked in a hospital shower, confused as hell, with no idea where I was or what had happened. A pretty solid metaphor for the next several years of my life, honestly.
I still don't know exactly what that "big job" is supposed to be. But I figure writing a book that might help people who are going through the same shit I went through—that's probably part of it. •••

What This Book Is This is a survival guide. Not a medical textbook—I'm not a doctor, and I'm definitely not going to pretend I understand all the fancy neurological terms for why my brain does the weird shit it does. But I'll explain what I've learned in plain English, because that's all I've got. Not an inspiration story—I hate that stuff. "Look at the brave disabled man overcoming his challenges!" Screw that. I'm not brave. I'm just a dude who lived. Some days I'm barely managing. Some days I'm doing pretty damn good. Most days I'm somewhere in between, forgetting why I walked into the kitchen and getting irrationally angry about it. This is a book about what TBI is actually like. The memory problems, the impulse control disasters, the sensory overload, the fatigue that hits you like a truck, the emotions that are basically drunk now even when you're stone cold sober. The relationships that fall apart and have to be rebuilt—sometimes more than once. The identity crisis of looking in the mirror and not recognizing yourself. And yeah, the humor. Because if you can't laugh at this stuff, you're going to be frustrated forever, and that's no way to live. •••

What This Book Isn't This book is not a replacement for actual medical care. If you have a TBI, go see a doctor. Ideally one who knows what they're doing with brain injuries. Get everything documented. Take the recovery seriously. This book is not going to tell you everything will be okay. It might be okay. It might be really hard for a really long time. I'm not going to lie to you—that's not helpful. This book is not going to be negative, though. I've been through enough shit that I could write a whole book of complaints. But that's not what you need. You need to know that other people have been where you are, and they made it through, and here's what they learned along the way.
That's what I'm here for. •••

The TBI Guy I say this phrase a lot now: "TBI guy." It's my little reminder to people. Because here's the thing about traumatic brain injury—it's invisible. I look fine. I look like a normal, healthy, middle-aged guy. I don't have a wheelchair or a missing limb or anything that tells the world, "Hey, cut this guy some slack, his brain is held together with duct tape and optimism." So people forget. They get frustrated when I forget things. They get confused when I say something inappropriate. They get annoyed when I have to leave a crowded place because my nervous system is about to melt down. And I get it—it's hard to remember that someone is injured when you can't see the injury. "TBI guy." That's me reminding them. And reminding myself. You might need your own version of that. Some way to signal to the world that you're doing your best with a brain that doesn't work the way it used to. It's not an excuse—it's an explanation. There's a difference. •••

Permission to Laugh Here's something I figured out pretty early on: humor is survival. If you can't see the humor in your situation, you're going to be serious about everything, and you'll never make true change because you'll be frustrated constantly. Trust me—I tried the frustrated route. It sucked. So yeah, this book is called "Shit For Brains." Because that's literally what I have. My brain got scrambled, and now I have to figure out how to live with that. And sometimes the only thing you can do is laugh about it. I'm going to tell you stories that are funny and stories that are sad and stories that are both at the same time. That's TBI life. You learn to hold those things together. When I forget why I walked into a room—for the fourth time in ten minutes—I have a choice. I can get angry and spiral into frustration. Or I can throw my hands up and say, "Shit! Where am I? What was I supposed to be doing?" and just keep moving. Most days, I choose the second one. Most days. •••

For the Caregivers This book isn't just for people with TBI. It's also for the people who love them. My wife Alisha has been through this whole journey with me. We've been married, divorced, married again, divorced again, and married again…and again. Yeah, really. TBI is hell on relationships. Neither of us knew what we were doing in the beginning. We made a lot of mistakes. We hurt each other. We almost gave up. But we didn't. And now we're happier than we've ever been. She's going to chime in throughout this book with her perspective—what it's like to be the caregiver, the spouse, the person who has to watch someone they love struggle. Her voice is different from mine. She's warmer, more patient, more put-together. But she's also honest about how hard it is.

If you're the caregiver, there's stuff in here for you too. Because you matter. You can't pour from an empty cup, and you can't take care of someone else if you're not taking care of yourself. I know that sounds like bumper sticker wisdom, but it's true. Also: don't give up on them. That's my main advice. DON’T give up on them. •••

What I Know Now Here's something I wouldn't have believed in those early days, when I was an adult child struggling to take care of myself, overwhelmed with everything, mentally exhausted all the time: I'd go through all that shit again just to be this person. The old me—SSgt Lewis, EOD technician, total hardass—didn’t really know how to truly care about people and have empathy. I didn't have true deep compassion. I was confident, sure. But I was also kind of a dick about it. Still caught up in my own story. The new me is different. Better, in a lot of ways. I'm humbled. I'm more present. I care deeper. I have a new love for life and a dedication to growing and bettering myself. My wife says I'm an inspiration, but I try to stay humble about it. I didn't choose this path. But I'm walking it. And I've learned things along the way that I couldn't have learned any other way. •••

How to Use This Book You can read this front to back, or you can skip to whatever chapter you need most. Each one covers a different aspect of TBI life: Memory (why you can't find the thing you just put down) Impulse control (why you said that thing you shouldn't have) Sensory overload (why the grocery store is basically a war zone) Cognitive changes (why everything takes longer now) Fatigue (why the nap is non-negotiable) Emotional regulation (why your feelings are drunk) Relationships (why your spouse became your nurse and how to fix that)

Pain (why the headache moved in permanently) Executive function (why paperwork is your enemy) The medical system (how to fight for what you need) Identity (learning and accepting who you are now) Each chapter has my story, some actual medical information in plain English, practical strategies that actually help, and a section for the people who love us. Take what works. Leave what doesn't. That's all any of us can do. •••

Let's Go Alright. You've read this far, which means your attention span is doing better than mine in the early days of recovery. Let's get into it. Take it slow if you need to. You don’t have to cram all this in your head all at once. I'm going to tell you everything I wish someone had told me when I was lying in that hospital bed, confused and scared and wondering if I'd ever feel like myself again.

Spoiler: you won't feel like your old self. That person is gone. But the new person? They can be pretty amazing. If you do the work. If you don't give up. If you keep pushing forward and build the person you want to be—because you can't go back to who you used to be. That's not negative. That's just true. And truth is what I've got. I may be a bit repetitive at times, that’s intentional for the TBI patient just FYI. Let's go. •••

Understanding TBI without the medical degree ••• There's a moment—and if you have TBI, you know exactly what I'm talking about—when you realize your brain sent you the wrong memo. Maybe you're standing in a room with no idea why you're there. Maybe you just said something that made everyone go quiet. Maybe you're crying at a commercial for car insurance and you don't know why. That moment when you think: what the hell happened to me? Let me tell you what happened to me. And then let me tell you what's probably happening to you. •••
The Day Everything Changed October 2013. I was driving to work on a dirt road outside Boise. I'd done that drive a hundred times. It was just another morning. I don't remember any of it.

What I've been told is this: I flipped my car—a blue Scion tC—several times. I was ejected from the vehicle. Someone found me unconscious in a field. I was clinically dead when the paramedics got there. They life-flighted me to the trauma hospital in Boise. The list of injuries read like a horror movie: • Shattered C-spine • Broken back • Broken ankle • Broken ribs • Collapsed lungs • Severe traumatic brain injury The TBI was the one that would change everything. Specifically, my frontal lobe got scrambled. That's the front part of your brain, right behind your forehead. It's responsible for some pretty important stuff—like impulse control, emotional regulation, decision-making, and personality. You know, the stuff that makes you you. The doctors told my wife they didn't know if I'd wake up. And if I did wake up, they didn't know who would be looking back at her.

The First Month I woke up. The whole first month is a blur. I remember fragments: Being tired. So unbelievably tired. Everything being too loud, too bright, too much. Bad hospital food. (Some things you remember no matter how scrambled your brain is.) Waking up confused. Going back to sleep. Waking up confused again. I remember my wife's face. I remember not always knowing who she was. I remember knowing I should know, and the fear that came with not knowing. I remember feeling like a child in an adult's body. Like someone had handed me the keys to a life I didn't know how to drive anymore.

What TBI Actually Is Okay, let's get into the medical stuff. I'll keep it simple because that's all my brain can handle, and honestly, that's probably all yours can handle too right now. Traumatic Brain Injury happens when your brain gets hurt by some kind of external force. Car accidents. Falls. Sports injuries. Getting hit in the head. Explosions (that's a big one for combat veterans). Your brain is soft—about the consistency of Jell-O. It floats inside your skull in fluid. When your head gets hit hard, or when your body gets thrown around violently, your brain slams against the inside of your skull. Sometimes it bounces back and hits the other side too. That impact damages brain cells. It can tear the connections between different parts of your brain. It can cause bleeding and swelling. And unlike a broken bone, you can't put a cast on it and wait six weeks. •••

The Severity Bullshit Doctors classify TBI into three categories: Mild TBI (also called concussion): Loss of consciousness for less than 30 minutes, confusion for less than 24 hours. Moderate TBI: Loss of consciousness for 30 minutes to 24 hours, confusion for 1-7 days. Severe TBI: Loss of consciousness for more than 24 hours, confusion for more than a week. Here's the thing about these labels: "mild" is a fucking lie. I've met people with "mild" TBI whose lives were completely derailed. Careers ended. Marriages destroyed. Years of struggling with symptoms that doctors dismissed because their injury was "just a concussion." If your brain got hurt and you're struggling, your injury is not mild. I don't care what the chart says. Your experience is valid. Mine was classified as severe, which at least meant people took it seriously. But I've learned that the label matters less than the reality of what you're living with every day.

Every TBI Is Different Here's something important to understand: no two TBIs are alike. Your brain is incredibly complex—billions of neurons connected in patterns that are unique to you. When it gets damaged, the specific symptoms depend on: • What part of the brain was injured • How severe the damage was • Your brain's individual wiring before the injury • Your overall health • Your age • About a million other factors So when you read this book, or any book about TBI, remember: your experience might be different. What works for me might not work for you. What I struggled with might not be your biggest challenge. That's okay. Take what helps. Leave the rest.

The Invisible Disability Problem Here's something that makes TBI extra special: nobody can see it. If I was in a wheelchair, people would understand. If I was missing a limb, they'd get it. But I look fine. I look like a normal, healthy guy. So when I forget something important, people think I'm not paying attention. When I say something inappropriate, people think I'm an asshole. When I have to leave a crowded place because I'm about to melt down, people think I'm being antisocial. When I'm exhausted after doing something that should be easy, people think I'm lazy. "But you look fine!" Yeah. That's the problem. You can't see the damage. You can't see the misfiring neurons, the broken connections, the parts of my brain that are working overtime to compensate for the parts that don't work right anymore.

It's like having a car that looks perfect on the outside but has a busted transmission. You turn the key and expect it to drive normally, and then it lurches and stalls and makes weird noises. But everyone looking at it thinks, "What's wrong with this guy? His car looks fine." ••• Different parts of your brain do different things. Here's a quick tour: • Frontal lobe (front of your brain): Decisionmaking, impulse control, emotional regulation, personality, planning, problem-solving • Temporal lobe (sides of your brain): Memory, language, hearing • Parietal lobe (top of your brain): Sensory processing, spatial awareness • Occipital lobe (back of your brain): Vision • Cerebellum (under the back): Balance, coordination

• Brain stem: Basic life functions (breathing, heart rate) My frontal lobe took the worst hit. That means my biggest challenges are: Impulse control: The filter between my brain and my mouth is broken. Thoughts become words before I can stop them. Emotional regulation: My emotions are basically drunk now. They're too big, too fast, too hard to control. I feel things intensely and express them immediately, which causes conflict with the people I love. Personality changes: I'm not the same person I was before the accident. In some ways, I'm better—more empathetic, more compassionate. In other ways, it's been a challenge for the people around me to adjust to who I became. Your injury might have affected different parts of your brain. Your challenges might be different. But whatever they are, they're real, and they matter.

The Statistics (You're Not Alone) Let me throw some numbers at you, because sometimes it helps to know you're not the only one: • About 2.8 million Americans go to the emergency room for TBI every year • TBI contributes to about 30% of all injury deaths • About 5.3 million Americans are living with TBIrelated disability right now • Males are about 1.5 times more likely to get TBI than females • The leading causes are falls (especially in older adults), car accidents, and being struck by objects • For military veterans, blast injuries are a major cause—about 20% of Iraq and Afghanistan veterans have experienced TBI That last statistic hits home for me. I served with guys who came back from deployment with TBI from explosions. Some of them are still struggling. The military culture of "toughing it out" means a lot of them didn't get help when they needed it.
If you're a veteran reading this: get help. Get everything documented. Don't suffer in silence. •••

What Recovery Actually Looks Like Here's what I wish someone had told me in those early days: Recovery is not linear. You'll have good days and bad days. Sometimes you'll feel like you're getting better, and then you'll have a terrible week. That's normal. Don't let the bad days convince you that you're not making progress. Recovery takes longer than you think. I'm over a decade out from my injury, and I'm still learning, still adapting, still growing. The doctors might tell you what to expect in the first year, but the truth is, your brain keeps changing and adapting for years. Recovery is not about getting back to who you were. I spent a long time trying to be the old Joe again. It doesn't work. That person is gone. Recovery is about becoming who you're going to be now—and that person might be pretty amazing, if you give them a chance.

You have to put in the work. The more you put into recovery, the more you'll get out of it. Take it seriously. Do the therapy. Learn the strategies. Test your limits. Don't stay stagnant thinking you're more limited than you are. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you're reading this and you're the spouse, parent, child, or friend of someone with TBI, here's what I want you to know: They didn't choose this. Whatever frustrating thing they just did—the forgetting, the outburst, the inappropriate comment—they didn't choose it. Their brain is injured. They're doing their best with broken equipment. It's going to be a long road. I know you want a timeline. I know you want to know when they'll be "back to normal." I can't give you that. Nobody can. What I can tell you is that things do get easier—but it takes time, and it takes patience.

What NOT to say: • "It'll get better." (We've heard it. It doesn't help. When? How? Give us something concrete.) • "But you look fine!" (We know. That's part of the problem.) • "Just try harder." (We're trying as hard as we can.) • "My cousin had a concussion and he was fine in a week." (Cool. That's not our experience.) What actually helps: • "I'm here." • "What do you need?" • "Take your time." • "I believe you." Take care of yourself too. You can't pour from an empty cup. Caregiver burnout is real. Eat. Sleep. Get support. Take breaks. Your needs matter too.

The Big Question After everything I've just told you—the accident, the injuries, the long road of recovery—you might be wondering “how can he say it was worth it?” I know. That sounds crazy. But it's true. Like I said earlier, the old me was confident but kind of a dick. I didn't have empathy, and I need that empathy now to help me understand my wife and what she goes through too. I didn't have real compassion. I thought I was tough, but I was actually just closed off. The new me is humbled. More present. More caring. I have a love for life that I didn't have before. I'm dedicated to continuously growing and getting better. Does that mean TBI is a gift? No. I'm not going to feed you that inspiration porn bullshit. TBI sucks. The accident sucked. The recovery sucked. A lot of days still suck. No way will I downplay the harsh reality. But I've made something out of it. I've become someone I actually like. And maybe that's enough. It’s my hope for you that you can find a silver lining too.

Coming Up In the next chapters, I'm going to get into the specific challenges of TBI life: • Memory • Impulse control (I've got stories) • Sensory overload • Cognitive changes • Fatigue • Emotional regulation • Relationships • Pain • Executive function • The healthcare system • Identity Each chapter has what happened to me, what's actually going on in your brain, and what might help. Plus sections for the people who love us, because they need this book too. But for now, just know this: whatever happened to you, whatever your TBI looks like, you're not alone.
Millions of us are walking this road. And we're going to figure it out together. Let's keep going.

sections.h: Chapter 2: Why Did I Walk Into This Room?
p: I'm standing in the kitchen. The refrigerator door is open. Cold air is hitting my face. I have absolutely no idea why I'm here. My wife just told me to get something. I know she did. It was like thirty seconds ago. But whatever it was has completely vanished from my brain, and now I'm just standing here like an idiot, staring at condiments and leftovers, hoping something will jog my memory. It doesn't. "Babe? What was I supposed to get?" She sighs. Not an angry sigh—she's used to this by now. Just a tired sigh. The sigh of someone who has answered this question a thousand times. "The butter." Right. The butter. Of course. It's right there. I grab it, close the fridge, and walk back to whatever we were doing.

If you have TBI, you know this moment. You've lived it dozens of times. Possibly hundreds. The walking into rooms with no idea why. The losing things you just had in your hand. The conversations that vanish from your brain before they're even finished. Welcome to memory after TBI. •••

The Filing Cabinet That Caught Fire Here's how I think about it: your memory is like a filing cabinet. Before TBI, everything had a place. You'd put something in, you'd take it out. The system worked. After TBI, someone set that filing cabinet on fire. Some of the folders are fine. Some are singed around the edges. Some are completely gone. And the filing system itself? Totally scrambled. So now you're trying to find things in a burned-out cabinet with no labels, and half the drawers are stuck, and sometimes you open a drawer looking for one thing and find something completely random from 1990. That's TBI memory.

What's Actually Happening in Your Brain Let's get into the medical stuff for a minute. Memory isn't just one thing—it's several different systems working together. And TBI can mess with any or all of them: Short-term memory (also called working memory): This is the stuff you're holding in your head right now. The thing your wife just asked you to get. The phone number someone just told you. The beginning of this sentence. TBI loves to mess with short-term memory. It's often the first thing to go. Long-term memory: This is the stuff that's been stored away. Your childhood. Your wedding day. Things that happened before the injury. Usually this is more protected—you might remember 1997 perfectly but have no idea what you ate for breakfast. Prospective memory: This is remembering to do things in the future. Take your meds at 2pm. Call the doctor tomorrow. Pick up milk on the way home. This one gets hit hard with TBI. The part of your brain most involved in forming new memories is called the hippocampus. It's deep in the temporal lobe, on both sides of your brain. When you learn something new, the hippocampus helps transfer it from short-term to long-term storage. TBI can damage the hippocampus directly, or it can damage the connections between the hippocampus and other parts of your brain. Either way, the result is the same: new information doesn't stick the way it used to. •••

The Coffee Guy Let me tell you about a guy I met in the hospital. He was a Navy First Sergeant. Got his TBI from getting hit in the head with a cue ball while breaking up a bar fight. Not exactly a heroic war story, but a TBI is a TBI. His memory lasted about five minutes. I mean that literally. Every five minutes, his brain reset. He'd have a conversation with you, and five minutes later, he'd have the exact same conversation again. Word for word. He was on repeat. The thing about this guy was, he loved coffee. And every few minutes, he'd forget he already had coffee and go get another one. The nurses tried to stop him—too much caffeine, upset stomach, he'd be up all night—but he'd forget they told him no and sneak around to get more anyway. My wife felt bad for him. One time she snuck him a Starbucks from outside. The nurses got onto her pretty good for that one. He'd stay up all night, wired out of his mind, stomach churning, and the next morning he wouldn't remember any of it. Then he'd start asking for coffee again. It was funny in a dark way. But it was also a reminder of how bad it can get. I was lucky. My memory came back. His might not ever. •••

My Memory Now Here's the thing: I'm over a decade out from my injury, and my memory has recovered a lot. The early days were rough—that first month is still mostly a blur—but my brain healed. Neuroplasticity is real. Recovery is possible.

But even now, there are things that stick with me from those early days. Habits I built. Workarounds I still use. And occasionally, when I'm tired or stressed, the old memory issues creep back in. If you're in the early stages of TBI, I want you to know: it can get better. It might not get all the way back to where it was, but your brain is capable of healing and adapting in ways that might surprise you. But you have to put in the work. You have to build systems. You have to be patient with yourself. •••

The Frustration Let me be real about something: memory problems are frustrating as hell. It's not just the inconvenience of forgetting things. It's the way it makes you feel. Stupid. Unreliable. Like you can't trust your own brain. You tell someone you'll do something, and then you forget, and they think you don't care. But you do care. You just... forgot. You have the same conversation three times because you don't remember having it, and people get annoyed. But what are you supposed to do? You don't know you already talked about this. You move something, and then you have no idea where you put it, and you spend twenty minutes looking for your keys that are in your hand. Your hand. Right there. The whole time. The most frustrating thing about memory issues is that you can't control it. You can't just "try harder" to remember. That's not how brain injuries work. The hardware is damaged. Willpower doesn't fix hardware. •••

What Actually Helps Okay, here's the practical stuff. The strategies that actually work: External memory systems: Stop trying to hold everything in your head. Your head is not reliable right now. Use your phone. Use calendars. Use notebooks. Use sticky notes. Use whatever works for you, but get the information OUT of your brain and INTO something that won't forget. Memory stations: Pick specific places for specific things, and NEVER deviate. Keys go on the hook by the door. Always. Wallet goes on the dresser. Always.

Phone goes on the charger. Always. If you always put things in the same place, you don't have to remember where you put them. Routine: The more you can put your life on autopilot, the less you have to remember. Same morning routine every day. Same order of operations. Routine is your friend. Music: This one is personal to me, but music helps me remember things. There's something about connecting emotions and memories to songs that makes them stick better. If I need to remember something important, sometimes I'll tie it to a song in my head. Repeat it back: When someone tells you something, repeat it back to them. "So you need me to pick up milk and call the doctor. Got it." The act of saying it out loud helps it stick, and it confirms you heard it right. Write it down immediately: Don't tell yourself "I'll remember this." You won't. Write it down right now. Right this second. Before it's gone.

Stop Fighting Your Brain Here's the biggest lesson I learned about memory after TBI: Stop fighting your brain. Work with it. I spent a lot of time in the early days being angry at my memory. Trying to force myself to remember things. Getting frustrated when I couldn't. Feeling like a failure. That doesn't work. You can't bully your brain into healing faster. What works is accepting where you are, building systems to compensate, and being patient with yourself. Your brain is injured. It's doing its best. You have to work with what you've got. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with TBI memory issues, here's what I want you to know: Don't take it personally when we forget. We didn't forget because we don't care about you. We forgot because our brain is injured. There's a difference. Help without making us feel stupid. There's an art to this. Gently reminding someone is helpful. Making them feel like an idiot for forgetting is not. We already feel bad enough. Be patient with repeated questions. We're not doing it to annoy you. We genuinely don't remember asking before. Help us build systems. Instead of getting frustrated that we forgot something, help us set up a reminder system so we don't forget next time. Understand the fatigue connection. When we're tired, our memory gets worse. If we've had a long day and we're forgetting everything, it's not personal—our brain is running on empty. •••
The Good News Here's what I want you to take away from this

chapter: Memory problems are one of the most common TBI symptoms. If you're struggling with this, you're not alone. Millions of people are dealing with the same thing. Memory can improve. The brain has more ability to heal and adapt than we used to think. I'm living proof. Systems work. You might not be able to fix your memory, but you can build workarounds that make life manageable. And on the days when you're standing in front of the refrigerator with no idea why you're there, just know: we've all been there. Every single one of us in this club has had that moment. You're not losing your mind. You're dealing with an injury. There's a difference. Now close the fridge before you let all the cold air out.

From My Wife’s Perspective The memory issues are no joke. Just this morning I sent my husband to make me a cup of coffee and he came out a few minutes later with nothing and I was just like “where’s the coffee?” and he had made it but forgot what he was doing and just came back to me.

We both laughed “TBI moment” and he went and got the coffee, no one got hurt and it was still piping hot. There is no need to fuss or fight over memory slips, it’s going to happen. Even people with no brain injury have moments like these from time to time and if you haven’t, wait until you get older. For the record I don’t regret getting the Navy Sergeant Starbucks coffee. He was so happy and grateful for five minutes, then he was back on the search for coffee. Try to be patient.

sections.h: Chapter 3: Did I Say That Out Loud?
p: I called my First Sergeant gay for drinking diet coke. I was in the hospital. Neck brace on. Broken everything. Barely knew what planet I was on. And this man—my superior officer, a guy who could have made my life very difficult—walked in with a diet coke, and the words just came out of my mouth. "You’re gay." Everyone went quiet. You know that silence. The one where everyone is looking at each other like "did he really just say that?" Yeah. I really just said that. Here's the thing: I didn't mean to say it. I didn't plan to say it. I didn't even really think it—not in any conscious way. It just... happened. The thought appeared in my brain and exited through my mouth without stopping at any of the checkpoints in between. That's what frontal lobe damage does. It takes your filter—that little voice that says "maybe don't say that out loud"—and throws it in the garbage. Welcome to impulse control after TBI.

The Brake Pedal Is Broken Let me explain what's happening in your brain. Your prefrontal cortex—the front part of your frontal lobe, right behind your forehead—is basically the brake pedal of your brain. It's the part that says "slow down" and "think about this" and "maybe reconsider before you do that." It handles: Impulse control (not saying/doing stupid things) Decision-making (weighing options before choosing) Social appropriateness (knowing what's okay in different situations) Emotional regulation (keeping your feelings in check) Judgment (knowing the difference between good and bad ideas) When your prefrontal cortex gets damaged, all of that goes haywire. The brake pedal stops working. Thoughts become words. Impulses become actions. And you're left standing there wondering why everyone is staring at you.
It's not a moral failure. It's not a character flaw. It's a brain injury. That doesn't make it less embarrassing. But it does explain why it happens. •••

The Horror of Hearing Yourself There's this moment—and if you have frontal lobe damage, you know exactly what I'm talking about— where you hear yourself say something and you think: "Fuck! Why did I say that?" It's like watching a car crash in slow motion, except you're the car. You can see it happening. You can hear the words coming out. But you can't stop it. And then it's out there. In the world. And you have to deal with the consequences. The horror isn't just the thing you said. It's the realization that you can't trust yourself. That your brain might betray you at any moment. That the filter you relied on your whole life to keep you out of trouble is just... gone. That's a terrifying thing to live with.

It's Not Just Words Impulse control problems aren't just about saying inappropriate things. They can show up in all kinds of ways: Verbal impulsivity: Saying things you shouldn't. Interrupting people. Oversharing personal information. Blurting out whatever's on your mind. Behavioral impulsivity: Doing things without thinking them through. Impulsive spending. Making big decisions on a whim. Acting before considering consequences. Emotional impulsivity: Reacting immediately to feelings. Anger that explodes out of nowhere. Tears that come without warning. Laughing at inappropriate times. For me, it's mostly the verbal stuff. My mouth moves faster than my brain can keep up. But I've talked to other TBI survivors who struggle more with the behavioral or emotional side. Whatever form it takes, the root cause is the same: the part of your brain that's supposed to pump the brakes isn't working right.

The Social Minefield Here's what makes impulse control problems extra hard: we live in a social world. Human interaction is full of unwritten rules. Things you're supposed to say. Things you're not supposed to say. Ways you're supposed to behave depending on who you're with and where you are. Before TBI, you probably navigated these rules without even thinking about it. Your brain just knew. Don't say that to your boss. Don't mention that at a funeral. Don't make that joke in front of your mother-in-law. After TBI, those automatic filters are gone. You have to manually process every social situation, trying to figure out what's appropriate, while your brain is throwing random thoughts at your mouth like a malfunctioning pitching machine. It's exhausting. And you're going to mess up. A lot. •••
What My Wife Does I'm lucky. I have someone who helps me navigate this.

My wife Alisha has become my external filter. She lets me know what's inappropriate—because otherwise, I wouldn't know. Especially in public, she helps me not embarrass myself. We've developed signals. Little looks or touches that mean "dial it back" or "maybe don't say the next thing you're thinking." It's not perfect, but it helps. If you have someone in your life who can do this for you, let them. It's not weakness to need help. Your brain is injured. Having someone watch your back is just smart. And if you're that person—the spouse, the friend, the family member who's playing the role of external filter—thank you. I know it's not easy. I know it's tiring. But you're making a real difference. •••

Strategies That Actually Help Okay, let's talk about what you can do to manage this. The internal monologue technique: This is my main strategy. Before I say something, I try to run it through my head completely. Like, actually narrate it internally. "I'm about to say X. Is X appropriate? How will people react to X?" It's like trying to manually recreate the filter that used to work automatically. Does it catch everything? No. Sometimes things still slip out before I can stop them. But it catches a lot more than if I wasn't doing it at all. The pause: When you feel the urge to say something, pause. Count to five if you have to. Give your slower, more rational brain a chance to catch up with your impulsive brain. Trusted person signals: Work with someone you trust to develop a signal system. A look, a word, a touch— something that means "check yourself" without embarrassing you in front of everyone. Know your triggers: For a lot of us, impulsivity gets worse when we're tired, stressed, or overstimulated. If you know you're in a vulnerable state, be extra careful. Maybe avoid social situations that are likely to trip you up. Apologize gracefully: You're going to mess up. It's going to happen. Learn to apologize quickly and sincerely. "I'm sorry, that came out wrong. My brain injury affects my filter. I didn't mean to offend you." Most people will understand.

Avoid alcohol: Look, I'm not going to tell you how to live your life. But alcohol lowers inhibitions even in people with fully functioning brains. If your filter is already broken, alcohol removes whatever tiny bit of filter you have left. Just be aware. •••

It's Neurological, Not Moral I want to make something really clear: If you have impulse control problems because of TBI, you are not a bad person. You have a brain injury. The part of your brain that's supposed to regulate this stuff is damaged. You're not choosing to say inappropriate things. You're not being rude on purpose. Your hardware is broken. That doesn't mean you get a free pass. You're still responsible for trying to manage it, for apologizing when you mess up, for working on strategies to improve. But you don't need to hate yourself for something you can't fully control. I spent a lot of time feeling like an asshole. Feeling like something was wrong with me as a person. It took a while to understand that this is a symptom, not a character flaw.

If you're struggling with that—if you're beating yourself up every time you say something you shouldn't—give yourself some grace. You're dealing with a brain injury. That's hard enough without adding self-hatred on top of it. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with TBI-related impulse control issues, here's what I want you to know: We don't mean it the way it sounds. Most of the time, anyway. The words that come out of our mouths don't always reflect what we actually think or feel. They're brain misfires, not deliberate attacks. We know. Right after we say something inappropriate, we usually know it. We can see it on your face. We can feel the awkwardness. We're not oblivious—we're just unable to stop it before it happens. It's okay to tell us. If we say something out of line, you can tell us. We'd rather know than walk around oblivious to the fact that we just offended someone. Help us without shaming us. There's a difference between "Hey, maybe dial it back" and "I can't believe you just said that, what's wrong with you?" One is helpful. The other makes everything worse. Know when to intervene. In social situations, sometimes we need you to step in. Change the subject. Pull us aside. Give us a signal. We might not be able to save ourselves, but you might be able to save us. •••

The Upside (Kind of) Here's a weird thing about losing your filter: sometimes the truth just comes out. And sometimes, that's not the worst thing. I've said things that needed to be said—things I would have kept to myself before the accident. I've been honest in situations where politeness would have been a lie. I've called out bullshit that everyone else was too polite to mention. Not always at the right time. Not always in the right way. But there's something to be said for a brain that doesn't know how to be fake. I'm not saying impulse control problems are a gift. They're not. They cause real problems in real relationships. But if you're looking for a silver lining, maybe it's this: the new you might be more honest than the old you ever was. For better or worse. •••

Keep Trying Look, I'm not going to pretend I've got this figured out. I still say things I shouldn't. I still have moments where everyone goes quiet and I realize I just put my foot in my mouth. I'm still working on it, more than a decade later. But it has gotten better. The strategies help. The awareness helps. Having people around me who understand helps. Your filter might be broken. But you can build a new one. It's slower, it's manual, it's not as good as the original. But it's something. And something is better than nothing.

sections.h: Chapter 4: Why Is Everyone So LOUD?
p: I'm in Walmart. I'm barely healed enough to be out of the hospital, but I wanted to feel normal for five minutes. That was a mistake. The fluorescent lights are buzzing. Not just buzzing— screaming. Every flicker feels like a strobe light pointed directly at my brain. The music overhead—some generic pop song I've heard a thousand times—is drilling into my skull. There are people everywhere, carts clanking, kids yelling, someone's phone going off, a baby crying three aisles over. And it's all coming at me at once. All of it. No filter. No buffer. Just a wall of sensory input slamming into my damaged brain. My heart starts racing. My skin feels wrong. I can feel the panic rising in my chest. I need to get out. I need to get out right now.

I abandoned my cart and headed for the exit. I don't even remember walking back to the rehab facility, but I was shaking, trying to breathe, wondering what the hell just happened to me. That was my introduction to sensory overload after TBI. •••

Your Brain Lost Its Bouncer Here's what's happening: Your brain is constantly being bombarded with sensory information. Sounds, lights, smells, textures, movement—every second, there's a flood of input coming in through your eyes, ears, nose, skin. Before TBI, your brain had a bouncer. A filter that stood at the door and said, "You're relevant, you can come in. You're not important, stay outside." The bouncer decided what got your attention and what got filtered out as background noise. That's why you could have a conversation in a crowded restaurant. That's why fluorescent lights didn't bother you. That's why you could walk through a busy store without feeling like the world was attacking you.

After TBI, the bouncer is gone. Or drunk. Or just really bad at his job. Now everything comes in. The relevant stuff and the irrelevant stuff. The conversation AND the music AND the lights AND the guy coughing across the room AND the weird smell from the food court AND the pattern on the carpet AND the buzz of the electricity in the walls. Your brain can't sort it out. It's overwhelmed. And it responds the only way it knows how: panic. •••

What Sets It Off Everyone's triggers are different. For me, the big ones are: Crowds. This is my biggest one. Lots of people moving, talking, existing in the same space. It's too much input from too many sources. Sharp unexpected noises. A dog barking. A kid screaming. A car horn. Anything sudden and loud that my brain wasn't prepared for. It hits like a physical blow.

Fluorescent lights. Something about the flicker—even when you can't consciously see it—messes with my brain. Busy visual environments. Stores with too much stuff. Bright colors everywhere. Movement in every direction. My eyes don't know where to look, and my brain doesn't know how to process it. Multiple conversations. When there's more than one person talking at once, I can't filter. I'm trying to listen to all of them and none of them at the same time. You might have different triggers. Maybe it's certain sounds, or certain types of light, or certain textures. Part of living with this is figuring out what sets you off. •••

What It Feels Like If you don't have TBI, you might not understand what sensory overload actually feels like. Let me try to explain. It's not just "being annoyed by noise." It's not "preferring quiet." It's a full-body response that feels like an emergency.

Your heart rate spikes. You start to sweat. Your muscles tense up. Your brain is screaming at you to get out, get away, make it stop. It's like your nervous system is convinced you're in danger, even though logically you know you're just in a grocery store. The rational part of your brain is saying "this is fine" while the survival part is screaming
"WE'RE UNDER ATTACK."

And the more input keeps coming, the worse it gets. It builds and builds until you either escape or you melt down. A meltdown can look like a lot of things. For some people, it's crying. For some, it's anger. For some, it's shutting down completely—going quiet, going blank, checking out. For me, it's this frantic need to escape, followed by exhaustion so deep I can barely move. It's embarrassing. It's exhausting. And until it happened to me, I had no idea it was even possible. •••
The Science Part Let me get a little technical for a second.

The part of your brain that handles sensory processing is called the thalamus. It's like a relay station— information comes in from your senses, goes through the thalamus, and gets routed to the appropriate part of your brain for processing. When the thalamus or its connections are damaged, the routing gets messed up. Too much information gets through. Things that should be filtered out as "not important" get flagged as urgent. Your brain is trying to process everything at once, and it doesn't have the resources. On top of that, TBI often causes something called "central sensitization." Your nervous system becomes hypersensitive. Things that wouldn't have bothered you before now feel amplified. Sounds are louder. Lights are brighter. Touches are more intense. It's not in your head. Well, technically it is—it's literally in your brain. But you're not imagining it. Your sensory experience has genuinely changed. •••
The Shame Can I be honest about something? There's shame in this.

Leaving a store because the lights were too bright. Asking people to talk quieter. Avoiding restaurants, concerts, parties—places that normal adults go without a second thought. It feels weak. It feels broken. It feels like something you should be able to just "get over." I've had people look at me like I'm crazy. Like I'm being dramatic. Like I just need to toughen up. I've looked at myself that way too. But here's what I've learned: this is a real symptom of a real brain injury. It's not weakness. It's not drama. It's your brain telling you that it's overwhelmed and it needs relief. You wouldn't tell someone with a broken leg to "just walk it off." Don't tell yourself to just "deal with" sensory overload. •••

What Actually Helps Okay, let's talk strategies. Headphones. This has been a game-changer for me. Noise-canceling or noise-isolating headphones can block out a lot of the auditory chaos. I prefer over-the61 ear, but even earbuds help. Sometimes I wear them even without music playing, just to dampen the world. Sunglasses. And not just outside. If fluorescent lights bother you, sunglasses inside a store are a legitimate strategy. Yeah, you might look like a weirdo. Who cares. There are also special FL-41 tinted lenses designed for light sensitivity—look into those if this is a big problem for you. Know your limits. This is huge. There are times when I can handle more stimulation, and times when I can't. If I'm rested and calm, I might be okay in a moderately busy environment. If I'm tired or stressed, even a quiet room can feel like too much. Be honest with yourself about where you are. Plan your exits. Before you go somewhere, think about how you'll escape if you need to. Where are the doors? Where can you go to get away from the noise? Having a plan reduces the panic. Go at off-peak times. Grocery shopping at 10pm is a lot different than grocery shopping on Saturday afternoon. If you have flexibility, use it. Take breaks. If you're in an overwhelming environment and you can't leave, find somewhere to take a break. A quiet corner. A bathroom. Your car. Even five minutes of reduced input can help you reset. Be honest with people. "I have a brain injury and loud environments are hard for me." Most people will understand. And if they don't, that's their problem. •••

Grocery Pickup/Delivery Is Not Giving Up I want to say this clearly: Using accommodations is not weakness. If grocery pickup means you don't have a meltdown in the cereal aisle, use grocery pickup. If wearing headphones in public means you can actually function, wear headphones in public. If you need to leave a party early because it's too loud, leave the party early. You're not giving up. You're not being a baby. You're managing a disability. That takes more strength than "toughing it out" ever could.

It Can Get Better Here's some good news: for a lot of people, sensory issues improve over time. The brain is adaptable. As it heals, it often gets better at filtering input again. Things that were unbearable in the first year might be manageable by year three. It's not guaranteed, and it's not always complete, but improvement is possible. You can also build tolerance through gradual exposure. Not by throwing yourself into the worst environments—that'll just traumatize you—but by slowly, carefully, pushing your limits a little at a time. Over time, your brain can learn to handle more. I'm a lot better now than I was in those early days. Walmart is still not my favorite place, but I can get through it. Crowds still bother me, but I can manage them with the right strategies. The world doesn't feel quite as aggressive as it used to.

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with TBI-related sensory issues, here's what I want you to know: It's not antisocial. When we leave events early or avoid crowded places, it's not because we don't want to spend time with you. It's because our brains literally cannot handle the environment. Help us escape gracefully. If you see us starting to struggle, help us get out without making a big deal of it. "Hey, let's go get some air" is a lot better than "What's wrong with you?" Create calm environments. At home, think about lighting, noise levels, visual clutter. A calm space to retreat to makes a huge difference. Don't push us to "just deal with it." We're not being dramatic. We're not weak. We have a brain injury that makes sensory processing difficult. Pushing us into overwhelming situations doesn't help us get better—it just makes us feel unsupported.
Believe us. If we say it's too loud, it's too loud—for us. Your experience of the environment is different from ours. Trust that we know what we're feeling. •••

The World Didn't Get Louder Here's the thing to remember: The world didn't get louder or brighter or more chaotic. Your brain just lost its ability to filter it out. That's not a character flaw. That's an injury. And like any injury, you can learn to work with it. You can find strategies. You can build accommodations into your life. You can get better at recognizing the warning signs and getting yourself to safety before the meltdown hits. You might never be able to walk through a crowded store like you used to. But you can figure out how to live in the world as it is, with the brain you have now. That's not giving up. That's adapting. And adapting is survival.

sections.h: Chapter 5: I Used to Be Smart
p: There's a lot more indecision now. That's the simplest way I can describe what happened to my brain. Before the accident, I knew things. I decided things. I moved through life with a kind of automatic confidence that I didn't even notice until it was gone. After the accident, I was uncertain about everything. I remember standing in my own house, in my own life, feeling like someone had handed me the keys to a car I didn't know how to drive. An adult child, told to take care of myself, overwhelmed with everything. Everything felt impossible. Every decision felt monumental. And I was so mentally exhausted, all the time, that even figuring out what to eat for dinner felt like climbing a mountain. •••
The Vertical Mountain In those early days, recovery felt like looking up at a vertical cliff face.

Not a gentle slope. Not a challenging hike. A straightup wall of rock, and someone was telling me to climb it with no gear and no experience. How was I supposed to function? How was I supposed to work? How was I supposed to be a husband, a person, anything at all, when my brain couldn't even get through a simple task without short-circuiting? I didn't feel dumb, exactly. That's not the right word. I felt overwhelmed. I felt tired. I felt like I was trying to run a marathon through quicksand. The old me could handle ten things at once. The new me could barely handle one. •••

What's Actually Happening Let me explain what's going on in your brain when you have cognitive changes after TBI. It's not that you've lost intelligence. Your IQ is probably still the same as it was before. But the speed and efficiency of your thinking? That's what takes a hit. Processing speed: Everything takes longer. The information comes in, and your brain needs more time to make sense of it. You're not dumber—you're slower. And in a world that expects quick responses, slower feels like failure. Attention and concentration: Staying focused is harder. Your brain gets distracted more easily, pulled in different directions, unable to lock onto one thing and stay there. Executive function: This is the stuff we'll talk about more in a later chapter—planning, organizing, problem-solving. The "CEO" functions of your brain. When these are impaired, even simple tasks feel overwhelming. Word-finding: You know the word. It's right there. You can almost see it. But you can't grab it. It's stuck behind a wall of fog, and by the time you find it, the conversation has moved on. Mental fatigue: Your brain is working harder than it used to. Every task requires more effort. And that effort drains you faster than it should. The result is that you feel like you're wading through mud while everyone else is walking on solid ground. •••

"I Know the Answer, I Just Can't Get There" This is the phrase I heard over and over from other TBI survivors. And it perfectly describes the experience. The knowledge is still in there. The intelligence is still in there. But the pathways to access it are damaged. It's like having a library full of books but half the lights are out and someone rearranged all the shelves. You know you know this. You've known it your whole life. But right now, in this moment, you can't get to it. And then, five minutes later, when the pressure is off, it comes to you. Of course. Obviously. Why couldn't you think of that before? Because your brain is injured. That's why. •••
The Grief I'm going to say something that might be hard to hear: You need to grieve your old brain.

I know that sounds dramatic. But it's true. The brain you had before the injury is gone. The way you used to think, the speed you used to process, the confidence you used to have—some of that is not coming back. And that's a loss. A real loss. It's okay to be sad about it. I spent a lot of time in the early days trying to be my old self. Trying to force my brain to work the way it used to. Getting frustrated and angry when it wouldn't. That doesn't work. You can't bully your brain into being undamaged. What works is grieving what you lost, accepting where you are, and figuring out how to move forward from here. •••

What Actually Helps Let me give you some practical stuff. Give yourself more time. Stop expecting yourself to be as fast as you were. Build in extra time for tasks. Reduce the time pressure where you can.

Write everything down. Your brain can't hold as much as it used to. Stop trying to keep everything in your head. Get it on paper, get it in your phone, get it somewhere external. One thing at a time. Multitasking is dead. Your brain can't do it anymore. Focus on one task, finish it, then move to the next. Sequential, not simultaneous. Test your limits. Here's something I learned: I stayed stagnant for a long time thinking I was more limited than I was. When I finally pushed myself, I found out I was more capable than I thought. Don't assume you can't do something until you've tried. Cognitive rehabilitation. This is a real thing. Therapists who specialize in TBI can help you retrain your brain, develop compensatory strategies, and improve functioning. Look into it. Take the recovery seriously. The more you put in, the more you'll get out. This isn't a passive process. You have to work at it. •••

When Grief Becomes Depression One more thing I need to say: There's a difference between grieving your cognitive changes and being clinically depressed. Grief is normal. Sadness about what you've lost is appropriate. But if you're stuck there—if you can't see any hope, if you can't function, if the darkness won't lift—that might be depression. Depression is extremely common after TBI. Something like 25-50% of TBI survivors experience it. It's not a character flaw. It's a medical condition that often accompanies brain injury. If you think you might be depressed, get help. Talk to a doctor. Talk to a therapist. This is treatable. You don't have to stay in that dark place. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with TBI-related cognitive changes, here's what I want you to know: Don't finish our sentences. I know we're slow. I know you can see where we're going before we get there. But jumping in and finishing our thoughts makes us feel incompetent. Give us time to get there ourselves.

We're still in here. The person you love is still there. They're just working with damaged equipment. The thoughts are the same; the delivery system is broken. Patience when we're processing. If we go quiet, if we seem like we're struggling, we probably are. Give us space to work through it without pressure. Celebrate the improvements. When we do something well, when our brain is working, acknowledge it. We need those wins. Don't compare us to before. We already do that enough ourselves. Comparing us to who we were just makes us feel worse about who we are now. •••

You're Not Stupid Let me end this chapter with something I wish someone had told me in those early days: You're not stupid. You're injured. There's a difference. An injured brain is not a broken person. It's a brain that needs time, and strategies, and patience, and some professional help. It's a brain that might heal more than you expect. It's a brain that can adapt and compensate and find new ways to function. You might never think exactly the way you used to. But you can think. You can learn. You can grow. And the person you become on the other side of this? They might surprise you.

Let me describe TBI fatigue for you. It's like being drunk but sober. So much mental fog. Anything you try to think about is static. Your brain is wrapped in cotton. The world is happening around you, but you're watching it through a dirty window, and you can't quite make sense of any of it. That's what fatigue feels like after TBI. And let me tell you something important: You cannot push through it. •••

Not Regular Tired I need you to understand something: TBI fatigue is not the same as regular tiredness. Regular tired is what you feel after a long day. You sleep, you wake up, you're better. Coffee helps. A second wind is possible. You can push through if you really need to. TBI fatigue is different. It's not just your body being tired. It's your brain being exhausted. And when your brain is exhausted, everything stops working. Your memory gets worse. Your processing slows down. Your emotions get harder to control. Your filter (if you have any left) disappears completely. Regular tired is like your phone being at 20% battery. TBI fatigue is like your phone being at 2%—and instead of a warning, it just shuts off without asking. •••

What's Happening in Your Brain Here's the medical explanation: Your brain was damaged. And a damaged brain has to work harder to do the same tasks it used to do easily. Think about it like a computer running on a damaged processor. Before the injury, your brain could run multiple programs efficiently, switching between tasks, processing information in the background. It was optimized.

After the injury, that optimization is gone. Every task requires more processing power. Every thought takes more energy. Your brain is working overtime just to do the basic stuff, and it runs out of fuel way faster than it used to. On top of that, TBI often affects the parts of your brain that regulate sleep and wakefulness. The hypothalamus, the hormonal systems, the whole sleepwake cycle can get disrupted. So not only are you using more energy during the day, you might not be getting quality rest at night. It's a double hit. More energy expenditure, less energy recovery. •••

I Can't Nap on Purpose Here's something weird about my fatigue: I can't nap intentionally. I can't just decide to take a nap and then fall asleep. My brain doesn't work that way. But sometimes, out of nowhere, I'll just knock out. Like someone flipped a switch. I'll be sitting on the couch, or in a chair, and suddenly I'm gone. Passed out from neural fatigue.

It's not a choice. It's not a decision. It's my brain saying "we're done" and shutting down whether I like it or not. And then I wake up, and I feel a little better. Not great, but better. Enough to keep going for a while longer. •••

You Cannot Push Past It Let me say this clearly: you cannot push past TBI fatigue. I know. You want to. You've got things to do. People are counting on you. You don't have time to be tired. I get it. But here's what happens when you try to push through: Everything gets worse. Your symptoms amplify. Your memory tanks. Your filter vanishes. Your emotions go haywire. You become a worse version of yourself, and you still don't get anything useful done because your brain is running on fumes. And then you crash even harder. You don't just need a rest—you need a full recovery period. What would have been a twenty-minute break turns into a day-long shutdown. Pushing through doesn't work. I've tried. Every TBI survivor I know has tried. It doesn't work. The fatigue wins. Every time. •••

The Headaches I need to mention this: for me, fatigue and headaches are connected. When I get really fatigued, the headaches come. And not just regular headaches—the kind that make you vomit. The kind that send you to a dark room for hours. The kind that feel like your brain is trying to escape through your eye sockets. Tylenol helps a little. But mostly, I have to sleep it off. There's no pushing through a headache like that. You just have to surrender to it and wait. If you're getting headaches with your fatigue, pay attention. Your brain is telling you something. It's telling you that you've pushed too far, waited too long, ignored too many warning signs. Listen to it. I know it's annoying. But listen.

The Energy Envelope Let me teach you a concept that helped me: the energy envelope. Think of your daily energy as an envelope. Before TBI, that envelope was big—you could fit a lot of activities in there. Work, socializing, errands, exercise, hobbies. Plenty of room. After TBI, the envelope is smaller. A lot smaller. You have to choose what fits inside. If you try to stuff too much in, the envelope tears. You crash. You pay for it later—sometimes for days. So you have to make choices. What's essential? What can wait? What can you skip entirely? What can someone else do for you? Living within your energy envelope isn't giving up. It's strategy. It's knowing your limits and working within them so you can actually function instead of constantly crashing.

What Actually Helps Here's the practical stuff: Rest before you crash. Don't wait until you're completely empty. Schedule rest breaks throughout your day, even if you don't feel tired yet. Preventive rest is way more effective than emergency rest. Learn your warning signs. For me, it's certain kinds of mental fog, difficulty finding words, increased irritability. Your warning signs might be different. Figure out what they are and take them seriously. Prioritize sleep. Whatever you need to do to get better sleep, do it. Sleep hygiene matters more now than it ever did before. Dark room, cool temperature, consistent schedule, no screens before bed—all of it. Pace yourself. Don't front-load your day with all the hard stuff. Spread activities out. Alternate between demanding tasks and easier ones. Give your brain breaks. Say no. This is hard, especially if you used to be someone who said yes to everything. But you can't do everything anymore. Saying no to some things means saying yes to having enough energy for the things that matter. Strategic napping. If you can nap (some of us can't do it on demand), a 20-30 minute nap in the early afternoon can help. But not too late in the day, or it'll mess with your nighttime sleep. Get a sleep study. If you're not sleeping well at night, it might be worth getting checked out. Sleep disorders are super common after TBI. There might be a treatable issue. •••

The Power of Saying No I want to expand on this one because it's important. Before my injury, I was a "yes" person. Can you do this? Yes. Can you help with that? Yes. Can you take on this extra responsibility? Yes. After TBI, I had to learn to say no. Not because I didn't want to help. Not because I didn't care. But because saying yes to everything meant saying yes to crashing, saying yes to being useless, saying yes to making everything worse. No is a complete sentence.

"Can you come to this event?" No. "Can you take on this project?" No. "Can you stay late?" No. You don't always have to explain. You don't have to justify your limitations. You can just say no and protect your energy for the things that actually matter. It feels selfish at first. It's not. It's survival. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with TBI fatigue, here's what I want you to know: The nap is not laziness. When we need to rest, we need to rest. It's not optional. It's not us being difficult. It's a medical necessity. Don't over-schedule us. Back-to-back activities might seem efficient, but for us, they're a recipe for disaster. Build in rest time between things. Watch for the warning signs. Sometimes we don't notice we're fading until it's too late. If you see us getting foggy, irritable, slow—suggest a break. Help us take care of ourselves. Understand the crash. If we push too hard and crash, we're not being dramatic. We're not milking it. Our brain literally ran out of fuel and needs time to recover. Let us say no. Don't guilt us for turning things down. Don't make us feel bad for not being able to do what we used to do. Support our need to protect our energy. •••

Your Battery Is Smaller Now Here's the bottom line: Your battery is smaller now. That's not a character flaw. That's brain injury. You can wish it was bigger. You can be frustrated that it's not. But wishing and frustration don't change the reality. What changes things is accepting the battery you have and learning to manage it. Charging it more often. Using it more wisely. Not running it down to zero because you're trying to pretend everything is normal.

Everything is not normal. You have a brain injury. Your energy is limited. Work with what you've got. The nap is non-negotiable. The rest is non-negotiable. Taking care of yourself is non-negotiable. Everything else can wait.

From My Wife’s Perspective If you had an active life before your loved one was injured, it can be hard to understand that you have to change to accommodate their energy levels. Even something as simple as going to a movie at the theatre can be too demanding. I didn’t learn this until Joe passed out from a combination of overstimulation and neural fatigue. They may need a lot more sleep than you think is “normal”. Sometimes Joe sleeps for 14 plus hours. I try not to wake him anymore; I understand that he is healing. When he says he’s tired I know he means it. When he’s rested, he functions better and is in a much better mood. Let your loved one get as much sleep as they can so they can heal.

It's harder to hold back my emotions now. That's the simplest way I can say it. Whatever I'm feeling, it comes out. Immediately. Intensely. Whether I want it to or not. And here's the thing that kills me: it causes conflict and hurt feelings with the people I love. The people I care about most. The people who least deserve to be on the receiving end of whatever my brain just decided to launch at them. I don't want to raise my voice. I don't want to snap. I don't want to have these intense reactions to things that shouldn't be a big deal. But my brain doesn't ask permission anymore. The emotion shows up, and it's out of my mouth before I can catch it. My emotions are basically drunk now. They're sloppy, unpredictable, way too loud, and they have no idea what's appropriate for the situation. Welcome to emotional regulation after TBI.

The Frontal Lobe Problem (Again) Remember how I talked about the prefrontal cortex being the brake pedal for impulse control? Well, it's also the thermostat for your emotions. In a healthy brain, your limbic system (the emotional center) generates feelings, and your prefrontal cortex regulates them. It turns the temperature up or down. It decides how much emotion is appropriate for the situation. It keeps things in a reasonable range. When your frontal lobe is damaged, that thermostat breaks. Your limbic system is still generating emotions—maybe even more intensely than before. But the thing that's supposed to regulate them? Gone. Damaged. Offline. So the emotions come in hot, and there's nothing to cool them down. No buffer. No brake. No "maybe let's think about this before we react." It's not that you're feeling things you shouldn't feel. The emotions are often valid—anger, frustration, sadness, joy. The problem is the intensity and the speed. Everything is dialed up to 11, and it happens instantly.

What It Actually Looks Like For me, emotional dysregulation shows up in a few ways: Immediate expression. I feel something, I say something. There's no gap between the emotion and the reaction. Whatever's happening inside is immediately happening outside. Intensity that doesn't match the situation. Something small happens, and I react like it's a big deal. My brain doesn't accurately calibrate how much emotion is appropriate. A minor frustration triggers major anger. A small disappointment brings overwhelming sadness. Getting stuck. When I get angry, I get angry and I stay angry. I stew about it. I can't just let it go and move on. The emotion grabs hold and won't let go for a long time. Conflict. Because I'm expressing intense emotions immediately, I end up in conflict with people. Arguments start over nothing. Feelings get hurt. Relationships get strained.

I Still Blow Up I want to be honest with you: I still blow up. Regularly. This isn't a "here's how I conquered emotional regulation" chapter. I haven't conquered it. I'm still working on it, more than a decade later. Some days are better than others. Some situations are easier than others. But the explosions still happen. The anger still comes. The intensity is still there. What's changed is how I handle the aftermath. And maybe how quickly I can recognize what's happening and try to do something about it. But cured? No. This is something I manage, not something I've fixed. •••

What Helps Me Let me tell you what I've learned: Keeping a calm environment. This is huge for me. The more predictable and controlled my environment is, the better I do. Random elements throw me off. Chaos feeds the emotional dysregulation. When I can control my surroundings, I can better control my reactions. Taking out the random elements. Unexpected things are triggers. Surprises—even good ones—can set me off. The more I can reduce the unexpected stuff in my life, the more stable I feel. Making life predictable. Routine helps. Knowing what's coming helps. Structure helps. When I know what to expect, my brain isn't constantly on high alert, ready to react to whatever comes next. Pacing and talking myself down. When I feel the anger rising, if I can catch it, I try to pace and talk myself down. Literally. Walking around, talking to myself, trying to get the rational brain back online before I say or do something I'll regret. Removing myself from the situation. Sometimes the best thing I can do is leave. Get out. Remove myself before it escalates. That's not weakness—that's strategy. I know what happens if I stay and keep engaging when I'm dysregulated. Nothing good.

The People Who Get Hurt Here's the hardest part: The people who get hurt by my emotional dysregulation are the people closest to me. My wife. My family. The people I love most. Strangers don't see this side of me as much. I can hold it together for short interactions. But the people who live with me, who see me every day, who are there when my defenses are down—they get the worst of it. And that's not fair. They didn't sign up for this. They don't deserve to be yelled at or snapped at or caught in the crossfire of whatever my brain is doing. I've hurt people I love with my reactions. I've said things I didn't mean. I've created conflict where there didn't need to be any. That's the cost of this symptom. And it's a heavy one. •••
The Guilt Can I be real about something?

The guilt is overwhelming sometimes. After an outburst, after I've hurt someone, after the emotion has passed and I can see clearly again—the guilt crashes in. Why did I say that? Why couldn't I control it? What's wrong with me? I know it's a brain injury. I know it's not entirely my fault. But knowing that doesn't erase the look on my wife's face when I've just unloaded on her for something that wasn't even her fault. The guilt doesn't help, either. It just adds another negative emotion on top of everything else. Guilt about the anger. Shame about the guilt. It spirals. Learning to forgive myself has been part of this journey. Not excusing the behavior—I'm still responsible for trying to manage it. But forgiving myself for having a damaged brain. For not being able to control something that's genuinely hard to control. •••

What the Doctors Call It Let me throw some medical terms at you: Emotional lability: Rapid, often unpredictable changes in emotion. Mood swings that happen fast and feel uncontrollable. Irritability: A lower threshold for frustration. Things that wouldn't have bothered you before now set you off. Affective dysregulation: The fancy term for what I've been describing. Your emotional responses don't match the situation appropriately. Pseudobulbar affect (PBA): This is a specific thing where people laugh or cry uncontrollably, in situations where it's not appropriate. Laughing at funerals. Crying at jokes. The emotion doesn't match the context at all. I don't have this, but some TBI survivors do. Why does this matter? Because if you can name it, you can talk to doctors about it. You can research it. You can find other people dealing with the same thing. Knowing the terminology helps. •••
Depression and Anxiety I need to mention this: emotional dysregulation often comes with depression and anxiety.

Depression affects something like 25-50% of TBI survivors. Anxiety affects 30-60%. These aren't separate from the brain injury—they're often caused by it. The same damage that affects emotional regulation can trigger clinical depression and anxiety disorders. If you're feeling hopeless, worthless, unable to enjoy things you used to enjoy—that might be depression. If you're constantly worried, on edge, unable to relax— that might be anxiety. These are treatable. Medication can help. Therapy can help. But you have to recognize it and get help for it. Don't assume that feeling terrible is just "part of TBI." Some of it might be a treatable condition on top of the TBI. •••

What Actually Helps (The Practical Stuff) Here's the strategy list: Know your triggers. What sets you off? Fatigue? Hunger? Certain topics? Certain people? Certain environments? The more you know your triggers, the more you can avoid or prepare for them.

Recognize the warning signs. For me, there are physical signs before an explosion. Tension in my shoulders. A certain feeling in my chest.
