If I can catch those signs early, I have a better chance of intervening. Have an exit strategy. Know how you're going to remove yourself if needed. "I need to take a walk." "I need a minute." "Let's pause this conversation." Have the words ready. Exercise. Physical activity helps regulate mood. It's not a cure, but it's a tool. Regular exercise can take the edge off. Limit alcohol. Alcohol destabilizes mood even in people with healthy brains. With a damaged frontal lobe, it makes everything worse. Be careful. Consider medication. There are medications that can help with mood regulation. SSRIs, mood stabilizers, other options. Talk to a doctor who understands TBI. Find a TBI-informed therapist. Regular therapy is good. Therapy with someone who understands brain injury is better. They can help you develop specific strategies for your specific challenges.

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with TBI-related emotional dysregulation, here's what I want you to know: It's not about you. Most of the time, anyway. When we explode, it often has nothing to do with what you did. You might be the target, but you're not the cause. The cause is a damaged brain. Don't match our energy. When we escalate, don't escalate with us. That makes everything worse. Stay calm if you can. De-escalate. Don't add fuel to the fire. It's okay to set boundaries. You don't have to tolerate abuse. You can say, "I understand you're upset, but I'm not going to be spoken to like that. Let's talk when you've calmed down." Protecting yourself is reasonable. Help us see the warning signs. Sometimes you can see it building before we can. A gentle "Hey, you seem tense, do you need a break?" can help us catch it before it explodes. Know when to insist on help. If the emotional dysregulation is severe, if it's damaging relationships, if it's making life unmanageable—push for professional help. Therapy. Medication evaluation. Whatever it takes. •••

Your Emotions Are Valid Let me end with this: Your emotions are valid. Even when they're too big. Even when they come out wrong. Even when they cause problems. You're not a bad person for having intense emotions. You have a brain injury that affects your ability to regulate them. That's a medical condition, not a character flaw. But—and this is important—valid emotions still require responsible management. You're still accountable for trying to get better at this. For apologizing when you hurt people. For building strategies. For getting help. The emotions are valid. The damage they cause still matters. Both things are true. Keep trying. Keep apologizing. Keep building better strategies. Keep working on it.
That's all any of us can do.

sections.h: Chapter 8: My Wife Became My Nurse
p: My wife and I have been married four times. To each other. Yeah. You read that right. Married, divorced, married again, divorced again, married again, divorced again, married again. Four weddings, three divorces, same two people. TBI is hell on relationships. And I'm not going to pretend we figured it out right away. We didn't. We failed spectacularly. Three times. It took us years to learn how to be married to each other after my brain changed. But we made it. We're still here. And we're happier now than we've ever been. If you're struggling in your relationship after TBI— whether you're the survivor or the spouse—I want you to know: it's possible to get through this. But it takes work. It takes learning. It takes more patience than either of you thinks you have. Let me tell you what we learned.

The Day Everything Changed (For Her) When I talk about my accident, I talk about what happened to me. The injuries. The recovery. The symptoms. But there's another side to that story: what happened to my wife. One day, she had a husband. A partner. Someone she'd built a life with. The next day, she had a patient. She's told me what those early days were like for her. The uncertainty. The fear. The doctors saying they didn't know if I'd wake up, and if I did, they didn't know who I'd be. And then I did wake up. And I was different. And she had to figure out how to love someone who looked like her husband but didn't always act like him. •••

From Her Side I asked my wife Alisha to share her perspective for this chapter. Here's what she said: The hardest part was feeling helpless and the uncertainty surrounding recovery. The doctors had no idea how much functioning or memory he would regain. My husband woke up in a childlike state, and they said he could be that way forever or slowly get better over time. That reality is very scary to be in. What people don't understand is that it's okay to have your own mixed emotions about the situation. I was angry, frustrated, scared, depressed, and so much more—all at once, the whole time. But being in a caring, loving role, your needs take the back burner. I wish people understood truly what it takes to be a caregiver and that others would offer more support. What no one tells you is that your loved one hates having to need you. It hurts their pride, and there's nothing fun about being a patient. •••

Neither of Us Knew Here's the truth: neither of us knew how to cope or deal with life after the accident. I didn't know how to be a person with TBI. She didn't know how to be a caregiver. We were both thrown into roles we never asked for and didn't understand.

We made mistakes. A lot of them. I was difficult. My emotions were all over the place. My filter was gone. I said things I shouldn't have said. I was exhausted and frustrated and grieving my old self, and I took it out on the person closest to me. She was overwhelmed. She was trying to take care of me while also dealing with her own feelings about what had happened. She was grieving too—grieving the husband she used to have, the life we used to have, the future we'd planned. We hurt each other. Not intentionally. But we did. •••

What Finally Worked The fourth time, we did it differently. We put in the effort. Real effort. Not just "trying harder" in a vague way, but actually learning how to take feedback, how to communicate clearly, how to speak our needs honestly. Clear and open communication. That's what saved us. Not assuming the other person knows what you need. Not expecting them to read your mind. Actually saying it, out loud, even when it's hard.

I had to learn to take feedback without getting defensive. When she told me something I was doing was hurting her, I had to listen instead of reacting. That's hard with a damaged frontal lobe. But it's necessary. She had to learn to speak her needs too. Caregivers often put themselves last. She had to learn that her needs mattered, that she was allowed to have them, that taking care of herself wasn't selfish. •••

She Still Loves Both of Me Here's something my wife said that stuck with me: From my perspective, she still loves the me that died that day, and the man I am now—and they aren't the same person. That hit me hard when she said it. She fell in love with one version of me. That version is gone. But she also fell in love with who I became. She holds both of those people in her heart. That's a kind of love I didn't know existed until I experienced it.

The Marine With No Visitors Let me tell you about someone I met in the hospital. There was a Marine in the room next to mine. TBI, like me. Bad one. He would throw fits. I could hear it through the walls— the nurses yelling "Devil dog, calm down!" while he raged. His brain was scrambled, and he didn't know how to handle it. But here's the thing that stuck with me: no one ever came to visit him. Not once. Not family, not friends, not anybody. He was alone in that hospital room, fighting a battle no one could see, with no one in his corner. I had my wife. I had my family. I had people fighting for me, advocating for me, making sure I got the care I needed. He had no one. And let me tell you something: patients who have no one don't get taken care of as well. That's just the reality. When you have someone there pushing for you, asking questions, holding staff accountable—you get better care. That Marine taught me something important: you have to have people fighting for you. And if you're the person fighting for someone else, you matter more than you know. •••

Advice for the TBI Survivor If you're the one with TBI, here's what I want to tell you: Your spouse is struggling too. This isn't just happening to you. It's happening to your whole relationship. They're grieving and scared and overwhelmed, just like you are. Try to have understanding. I know it's hard when your emotions are all over the place. But try. Speak your needs honestly. Don't expect them to read your mind. Tell them what you need, clearly and directly. Take feedback without exploding. When they tell you something isn't working, listen. Don't get defensive. They're trying to help.
Appreciate what they're doing. Being a caregiver is exhausting. Thank them. Acknowledge their sacrifice. Don't take them for granted. •••

Advice for the Caregiver If you're the caregiver, here's what my wife wants you to know: Don't feel guilty for anything. Just do your best and let others help you. Take care of yourself and be patient with your loved one. Your needs matter. You can't pour from an empty cup. You're not selfish for having needs. Get support. Take breaks. This is a marathon, not a sprint. It's okay to have mixed emotions. You can love someone and be angry at them. You can be devoted to their care and also be frustrated and exhausted. Those feelings can all exist at the same time. Find your own support system. You need people too. Friends, family, support groups, therapists—find your people. The caregiver needs care too.

What Saved Her I asked my wife what saved her sanity during those early days. She said: My military training and resilience is the only thing that helped me hold it together. And a lot of hope that he would get better. Every little win kept me going. She's an Air Force veteran, like me. That background— the discipline, the resilience, the ability to handle crisis—that's what got her through. But not everyone has that. And even with it, she barely made it. Caregiver burnout is real. The stress is enormous. Don't underestimate what caregivers go through. •••

How It Changed Her My wife says the experience changed her: I appreciate every little special moment now, as I know that life can change in a flash. I'm more grateful for everything. I do have more anxiety, especially about driving. I'm less selfish after learning to put someone else's needs first.

And here's what she says about who I became: He is much more compassionate, empathetic, and understanding after going through what he did. He has a new love for life and cares deeper, is more present, and is dedicated to growing and bettering himself. He is an inspiration to me, but he's humble most days. •••

Don't Give Up on Them My biggest piece of advice for caregivers is simple: Don't give up on them. I know it's hard. I know some days you want to walk away. I know they're not the person you knew, and you don't know if that person is ever coming back. But if you can hang in there, if you can learn together, if you can find new ways to love each other—there's something beautiful on the other side. We almost gave up on each other. Three times we called it quits. I'm so glad we were able to grow in that time apart and come back together stronger.

It Takes Two Here's the bottom line: TBI doesn't just happen to one person. It happens to the whole relationship. Recovery isn't just the survivor's job. It's both of your jobs. You have to learn together, adapt together, build something new together. The old relationship is gone. You can't get it back. But you can build a new one. Different, maybe. But maybe also deeper. More honest. More resilient. That's what we did. That's what you can do too.

sections.h: Chapter 9: The Headache That Moved In
p: In ••• The headache moved in after the accident and never left. I don't mean I have a headache sometimes. I mean pain became a permanent resident in my skull. Some days it's quiet, lurking in the background like a bad roommate you've learned to ignore. Other days it's screaming, demanding all my attention, making it impossible to think about anything else. And on the worst days—the really bad ones—it makes me vomit. Not nausea. Not "I feel a little sick." Full-on, head-inthe-toilet, can't-stop-heaving vomiting. From a headache. That's what severe post-TBI headaches can do. If you're dealing with chronic pain after TBI, you're not alone. And you're not being dramatic. This stuff is real.

Not Just a Headache Let me be clear about something: post-TBI headaches are not regular headaches. A regular headache, you take some Advil, drink some water, maybe lie down for a bit. It goes away. You move on with your day. Post-TBI headaches are different. They're more intense. They last longer. They come with other symptoms—light sensitivity, sound sensitivity, nausea, cognitive fog. And they don't always respond to the usual treatments. When someone says "it's just a headache," they don't understand what we're dealing with. This isn't "just" anything. This is a neurological symptom of brain damage, and it can be completely debilitating. •••

What's Causing This There are several reasons why TBI causes chronic headaches: Direct damage: The injury itself can damage structures in your head and neck that are involved in pain signaling. Nerves, blood vessels, muscles—all of it can be affected. Neck injuries: A lot of us who have TBI also have neck injuries. I shattered my C-spine. That kind of damage creates ongoing pain that refers to the head. Muscle tension: Your body responds to brain injury by tensing up. Chronic muscle tension in the neck, shoulders, and scalp can cause tension-type headaches that just don't quit. Nervous system changes: TBI can make your whole nervous system more sensitive. Pain signals get amplified. Things that wouldn't have caused pain before now hurt. Medication overuse: Here's a cruel irony—taking pain medication too often can actually cause more headaches. It's called medication overuse headache or rebound headache. You take something for the pain, it works temporarily, then it wears off and the headache comes back worse. Sleep problems: Poor sleep makes headaches worse. TBI causes sleep problems. It's a vicious cycle.

Types of Post-TBI Headaches Not all TBI headaches are the same. Here are the main types: Tension-type headaches: A dull, aching pain, usually on both sides of the head. Feels like a band squeezing your skull. This is the most common type after TBI. Migraine-type headaches: Throbbing pain, often on one side. Comes with sensitivity to light and sound, nausea, sometimes visual disturbances. These can be completely disabling. Cervicogenic headaches: Pain that starts in the neck and radiates up to the head. Common if you had neck injuries along with your TBI. Occipital neuralgia: Sharp, electric-shock-like pain in the back of the head. Happens when the occipital nerves are damaged or irritated. Mixed: A lot of us have more than one type. Lucky us. Knowing what type you have can help with treatment. Different types respond to different approaches.

The Vomiting Headaches I need to talk about this specifically because it's something people don't understand unless they've experienced it. When my headaches get really bad, I vomit. There's no stopping it. The pain gets so intense that my body just rejects everything. These aren't migraines in the traditional sense—I don't get auras or visual disturbances. It's just pure, overwhelming pain that builds and builds until my body can't handle it anymore. When these hit, there's nothing to do but ride it out. Dark room. No noise. No light. No movement. Just waiting for it to pass. Tylenol helps a little, if I can catch it early enough. But mostly, I have to sleep it off. Sometimes for hours. Sometimes for the rest of the day.

What Helps Here's what I've learned about managing chronic headaches: Tylenol (acetaminophen): This is my go-to. It takes the edge off without the risks of stronger medications. But you have to be careful not to take too much—it can damage your liver. Hydration: Dehydration makes headaches worse. Drink water. More than you think you need. Sleep: I know, I know—sleep is hard after TBI. But poor sleep makes headaches worse, which makes sleep harder, which makes headaches worse. Do whatever you can to improve your sleep. Dark, quiet rooms: When a bad one hits, reduce all stimulation. Light and sound make it worse. Give your brain a break from input. Ice or heat: Some people do better with ice on the head or neck. Some do better with heat. Try both and see what works for you. Preventive approach: Don't wait until the headache is a 10 to do something about it. When you feel it starting to build, take action early. Rest, medicate, reduce stimulation—whatever your strategy is, do it before it becomes unbearable. Identify triggers: Keep track of what seems to trigger your worst headaches. For me, fatigue is a big one. If I push too hard, the headache comes. Knowing your triggers helps you avoid them. •••

What About Stronger Medications? You might be wondering about prescription medications. There are options: Triptans: These are specifically for migraines. They can help if you have migraine-type headaches. Preventive medications: Beta-blockers, antidepressants, anti-seizure medications—these are taken daily to prevent headaches from happening in the first place. Nerve blocks: Injections that numb specific nerves involved in your headache pain. Botox: Yes, really. Botox injections can help prevent chronic migraines.

I'm not going to tell you what to take—that's between you and your doctor. But know that there are options beyond over-the-counter stuff. If your headaches are severely impacting your life, talk to a neurologist who specializes in headache or TBI. •••

Be Careful with Opioids I need to say this clearly: be very careful with opioid pain medications. Opioids can be effective for pain, but they come with serious risks. Addiction. Dependence. Making the pain worse over time. They can also mess with your cognition, which is already compromised after TBI. Some people need opioids for pain management, and that's a legitimate medical decision. But they should be a last resort, not a first line treatment, and they should be carefully monitored by a doctor. If you're taking opioids for chronic headaches, make sure you have a doctor who's paying attention and a plan for managing the risks.

The Pain Is Real Let me say something that might seem obvious but needs to be said: Your pain is real. I know some people act like chronic pain is all in your head. Like you're exaggerating. Like you should just tough it out. Those people don't know what they're talking about. Chronic pain after TBI is a well-documented medical phenomenon. It's neurological. It's physical. It's measurable. It's real. You're not weak for struggling with it. You're not making it up. You're dealing with a real symptom of a real injury, and it's hard, and you deserve support and treatment. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with chronic post-TBI headaches, here's what I want you to know: Take it seriously. When we say we have a headache, we're not talking about a minor inconvenience. We're talking about real, significant pain that affects our ability to function. Create a headache-friendly environment. Keep some spaces in the house quiet and dim. Have a plan for when a bad headache hits. Don't take it personally. When we're in pain, we might be irritable, withdrawn, or unable to do things we said we'd do. It's not about you. It's about the pain. Help us track patterns. Sometimes an outside observer can notice triggers that we miss. "You always get a bad headache after you skip lunch"—that kind of observation is helpful. Encourage treatment. If we're not getting adequate help for our headaches, encourage us to see a specialist. Sometimes we need a push to advocate for ourselves. •••
Living with the Roommate Here's the reality: chronic pain might be a permanent part of my life.

I've accepted that. Not happily, not easily, but I've accepted it. The headache moved in after the accident, and it might never move out. So I've learned to live with it. To manage it. To minimize it where I can and endure it when I can't. Some days are better than others. Some days I barely notice it. Other days it runs my whole life. But I'm still here. Still functioning. Still building a life despite the pain. You can too.

I can't clean anymore. I don't mean I don't like cleaning. I don't mean I'm lazy. I mean the mundane task of cleaning—something I used to do without thinking—has become almost impossible. I'll look at a messy room and know it needs to be cleaned. I can see the mess. I understand, logically, what needs to happen. But the steps between "this room is messy" and "this room is clean" have become this overwhelming, incomprehensible mountain. Where do I start? What do I do first? How do I break this down into steps? My brain just... stalls. It's like the engine won't turn over. That's executive dysfunction. And it's one of the most frustrating parts of TBI.

What Is Executive Function? Executive function is basically your brain's CEO. It's the set of mental skills that let you manage yourself and get things done: Planning: Breaking down a goal into steps and figuring out how to accomplish it. Organization: Keeping track of things, putting things in order, maintaining systems. Time management: Estimating how long things take, prioritizing, meeting deadlines. Task initiation: Starting tasks, even when you don't feel like it. Working memory: Holding information in your head while you use it. Flexibility: Adapting when things don't go as planned, shifting between tasks. Self-monitoring: Checking your own work, noticing mistakes, adjusting your approach. When your prefrontal cortex is damaged—which is what happens with frontal lobe TBI—all of these functions take a hit. The CEO of your brain is out sick, and nobody's running the company.

What It Looks Like Day to Day Let me give you some examples of how executive dysfunction shows up in real life: The cleaning thing: Like I said, I look at a mess and I freeze. I can't figure out where to start. The whole task feels like one giant, impossible thing instead of a series of small steps. Paperwork paralysis: Bills, forms, applications— anything that requires multiple steps and organization becomes a nightmare. I'll avoid it for weeks, knowing I need to do it, unable to make myself start. Cooking complexity: Following a recipe used to be easy. Now, keeping track of multiple steps, timing different things to be ready at the same time—it's overwhelming. I stick to simple stuff. Decision fatigue: Every decision, no matter how small, takes energy. What to eat, what to wear, what to do next—by the end of the day, I'm out of decisionmaking capacity. Losing track of time: I have no idea how long things take anymore. Something I think will take 20 minutes takes 2 hours. Something I think will take all day takes 20 minutes. My internal clock is broken. Starting is the hardest part: Even when I know exactly what I need to do, actually beginning feels impossible. I'll sit there, knowing I need to start, unable to start. •••

Being Overwhelmed with Too Much Here's what I've learned: being overwhelmed with too much makes TBI hell worse. The old me could juggle ten things at once. Handle a full plate. Multitask like a champion. The new me? I can handle what I can handle, and that's it. If I take on too much, everything falls apart. Not just the extra stuff—everything. My whole system crashes. So I've had to learn to limit my load. To say no to things. To keep my plate manageable instead of full. It feels like failure sometimes. Like I should be able to do more. But the reality is, doing less means doing it better. Overloading myself means doing everything poorly and feeling terrible.

The Overwhelm Spiral Let me describe what happens when executive dysfunction meets overwhelm: I have a task. Let's say it's cleaning the kitchen. My brain looks at the kitchen and sees: dirty dishes, cluttered counters, stuff that needs to be put away, the floor needs sweeping, the trash needs to go out... Instead of seeing individual tasks, my brain sees ONE GIANT IMPOSSIBLE THING. I feel overwhelmed. I don't know where to start. So I don't start. I walk away. Now I feel guilty for not doing it. The kitchen is still dirty. The guilt adds to the overwhelm. Tomorrow, the kitchen is worse. The overwhelm is bigger. The guilt is bigger. The spiral continues until the task feels so impossible that I can't even think about it without anxiety. This happens with everything. Cleaning. Paperwork. Projects. Life.

Breaking the Spiral So how do you break out of it? Make it smaller: Don't look at the whole kitchen. Look at ONE thing. "I'm going to put the dishes in the dishwasher." That's it. Just that. When that's done, maybe pick one more thing. Maybe not. One thing is better than nothing. External structure: Don't rely on your brain to organize things. Use lists, schedules, apps, reminders. Put the structure outside your head where you can see it. Body doubling: This is a thing where having another person nearby—not necessarily helping, just present— makes it easier to do tasks. Something about not being alone helps the brain engage. My wife's presence helps me start things I couldn't start alone. Timers: Set a timer for 10 minutes and do as much as you can. When the timer goes off, you can stop. Sometimes 10 minutes turns into more. Sometimes it doesn't. Either way, you did something. Routines: The more you can put on autopilot, the less executive function you need. Same routine every morning. Same routine for certain tasks. Routine is your friend. Lower the bar: Your standards might need to adjust. "Clean enough" is better than "not clean because I was waiting for perfect." Good enough is good enough. •••

Paperwork Specifically Paperwork deserves its own section because it's so universally hated among TBI survivors. Bills. Insurance forms. Applications. Tax documents. Medical paperwork. Every piece of paper requires: reading and understanding it, figuring out what action is needed, actually doing the action, filing or organizing the result. That's four executive function steps for one piece of paper. Now multiply that by all the paperwork in modern life. Here's what helps: One piece at a time: Don't look at the pile. Look at one piece of paper. Deal with that one. Then the next one.

Designated paperwork time: Instead of letting it pile up and then facing the mountain, schedule regular times to deal with paperwork. Even 15 minutes twice a week is better than facing a month's worth at once. Simple systems: Don't create elaborate filing systems you won't maintain. Simple is better. "To Do," "Done," and "File" might be all you need. Ask for help: If paperwork is truly beyond you, ask someone to help. A spouse, a family member, a friend. Some areas even have services to help disabled people with paperwork. There's no shame in needing help. Automate what you can: Auto-pay bills. Direct deposit. Paperless statements. The less paperwork that exists, the less you have to deal with. •••

The Judgment Can I be honest about something? There's a lot of judgment around executive dysfunction. People see a messy house and think you're lazy. They see unpaid bills and think you're irresponsible. They see unfinished projects and think you don't care.

They don't understand that your brain literally can't do these things the way it used to. I've judged myself too. Looked at a simple task I couldn't accomplish and thought, "What's wrong with me? This isn't hard. Why can't I just do it?" But it IS hard. For a damaged brain, these "simple" tasks require enormous effort. And sometimes, the effort just isn't there. It's not laziness. It's not lack of caring. It's neurological impairment. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you're the spouse, family member, or friend of someone with TBI-related executive dysfunction, here's what I want you to know: It's not laziness. When we don't do things, it's not because we don't care or don't want to. Our brains are struggling to initiate, organize, and complete tasks. Help us break things down. Instead of "clean the house," help us identify one specific task. "Start with taking out the trash." Small, concrete steps are easier than big, vague goals.

Don't add to the pile. Be mindful about how much you're asking us to manage. Adding more things to our plate when it's already full just makes everything worse. Celebrate small wins. Did we do one thing today? That's worth acknowledging. Progress is progress, even if it's slow. Offer to body double. Sometimes just being in the room while we do something helps. You don't have to do the task for us—your presence might be enough. Help with systems. If you're good at organization, help us set up simple systems that work with our limitations. •••

Working Within Limits Here's what I've come to accept: I have limits now that I didn't have before. I can't handle as much. I can't organize as well. I can't power through tasks the way I used to. Fighting against those limits doesn't make them go away. It just exhausts me and makes everything worse.

What works is accepting the limits and working within them. Doing what I can. Getting help with what I can't. Building systems that accommodate my brain instead of demanding my brain accommodate them. It's not giving up. It's being realistic. And being realistic is how you actually get things done. •••

One Thing at a Time If you take nothing else from this chapter, take this: One thing at a time. Don't look at everything you need to do. Look at one thing. Do that thing. Then look at the next thing. Your brain can't hold it all anymore. So don't try to hold it all. Put it on paper, put it in an app, put it anywhere outside your head. Then focus on one thing. One thing at a time. That's how you get through this.

sections.h: Chapter 11: The Doctors, the System, and the Bullshit
p: "It'll get better." That's what they tell you. Doctors, nurses, wellmeaning family members. "It'll get better." But fucking WHEN? Some mystery time in the future. Some vague "eventually." What about the now? What about today? What about the fact that I'm struggling right this second and "it'll get better" doesn't help me at all? That phrase drove me crazy in the early days. It still does. Because it's not advice. It's not help. It's a way to end the conversation without actually addressing what you're going through. This chapter is about dealing with the healthcare system—the doctors, the paperwork, the VA, the whole frustrating mess of trying to get help when your brain is already exhausted. And I'm going to be honest: it's hard. But I'm also going to tell you how to fight for what you need.

The Veteran Problem I'm a veteran. Air Force, seven years, EOD technician. And being a veteran creates a weird problem when it comes to healthcare. I'm locked out of a lot of civilian resources because I'm a veteran. There are programs, services, support systems out there for people with TBI. But a lot of them will turn you away if you're a veteran. "Oh, you have VA benefits? Go to the VA." They push you to the veteran system whether that system works for you or not. And when you go to the VA? You're surrounded by other veterans, some of whom are way more visibly injured than you are. Guys with missing limbs. Guys with caved-in skulls. Guys in wheelchairs. And there I am, looking like a normal healthy person, feeling like a fraud. I don't look injured. I look fine. So I feel like I'm taking resources from people who need them more. Even though I DO need them. Even though my brain is damaged too, just in ways you can't see.
That's the invisible disability problem all over again, but amplified in the veteran context. •••

My VA Experience I want to be balanced here, because my experience with the VA has actually been pretty good overall. The VA gets a lot of criticism, and some of it is deserved. The system is slow. The bureaucracy is frustrating. Getting appointments can be a nightmare. But the actual care I've received? It's been solid. The doctors have been knowledgeable. The treatment has been appropriate. I've gotten what I needed. Here's my advice about the VA: Be honest. Don't downplay your symptoms. Don't try to tough it out. Tell them exactly what's going on, even if it feels like complaining. Don't be afraid to speak up. If something isn't working, say so. If you need something you're not getting, ask for it. Advocate for yourself. Get everything documented. This is huge. Every symptom, every complaint, every conversation—make sure it's in your record. Documentation matters for your care, for your benefits, for everything. Don't go it alone. Lean on resources. Ask about support groups. Ask about programs you might not know about. The VA has more services than most people realize—but you have to ask. •••

The Civilian Healthcare Maze If you're not a veteran, or if you're using civilian healthcare alongside VA care, the system is its own kind of nightmare. Finding doctors who understand TBI. Getting insurance to cover what you need. Referrals and authorizations and pre-approvals. Fighting with billing departments. Waiting months for specialist appointments. All of this requires executive function. Paperwork, organization, follow-through, persistence. You know, all the things that TBI makes harder. It's a cruel irony: the injury that makes you need healthcare also makes navigating healthcare almost impossible.

Building Your Team Here's what I've learned: you need a team. A primary care doctor who understands TBI, or at least is willing to learn. This is your home base. Someone who knows your whole situation and can coordinate your care. Specialists as needed: Neurologist. Neuropsychologist. Physical therapist. Occupational therapist. Speech therapist. Pain specialist. Psychiatrist. You might not need all of these, but know they exist. A therapist who understands brain injury. Regular therapy is good; TBI-informed therapy is better. Someone who gets why your emotions are dysregulated, why your memory is shot, why you're struggling. An advocate—maybe your spouse, maybe a family member, maybe a patient advocate at the hospital. Someone who can help you navigate, push when you can't push, remember what you forget. You don't have to build this team all at once. Start with what you can get. Add people as you can.

How to Talk to Doctors Here's something I had to learn: how to communicate effectively with doctors. Write things down before your appointment. Your memory isn't reliable. Make a list of symptoms, questions, concerns. Bring it with you. Read from it if you need to. Be specific. "I feel bad" doesn't help them help you. "I have headaches three to four times a week, they're worst in the morning, and Tylenol only helps a little" gives them something to work with. Don't minimize. We have a tendency to downplay our symptoms, especially when we're talking to medical professionals. Don't do that. Tell them how bad it really is. Ask questions. If you don't understand something, say so. If you want to know why they're recommending something, ask. It's your brain. You're allowed to understand what's happening to it. Bring someone with you. If you can, bring your spouse or a family member to appointments. They can help you remember what was said, ask questions you forget to ask, and advocate for you if needed. •••

When Doctors Don't Listen Sometimes doctors don't listen. It happens. They dismiss your symptoms. They tell you it's anxiety. They rush through appointments. They don't take you seriously. This is frustrating as hell, but it's not the end of the road. Get a second opinion. You're allowed to see another doctor. If one doctor isn't helping, find one who will. Bring documentation. If you've been keeping track of your symptoms, bring that data. It's harder to dismiss when you have records. Be persistent. Sometimes you have to ask for the same thing multiple times before it happens. Keep asking. File complaints if necessary. If you're being genuinely mistreated, there are channels for that. Patient advocates. Hospital administration. Medical boards. You have options.
Find TBI-specialized providers. A doctor who specializes in brain injury is more likely to understand what you're going through than a general practitioner who's never dealt with TBI. •••

The Benefits Battle If you're trying to get disability benefits—whether through the VA, Social Security, or private insurance— prepare for a fight. The system is not designed to help you. It's designed to deny claims and save money. That's cynical but true. Here's what I've learned: Document everything. I've said this before and I'll say it again. Every symptom. Every limitation. Every way your TBI affects your daily life. The more documentation you have, the stronger your case. Get your doctors on board. You need medical professionals who will support your claim in writing. Clear statements about your diagnosis, your limitations, and your prognosis.

Be honest but thorough. When you're describing your limitations, don't downplay them—but also don't exaggerate. Be accurate. Describe your worst days, not just your average days. Appeal denials. Most people give up after the first denial. Don't. The appeals process exists for a reason. Many claims that are initially denied are approved on appeal. Consider getting help. There are lawyers and advocates who specialize in disability claims. If your claim is complex or has been denied, professional help might be worth it. •••

The Exhaustion of Fighting I need to acknowledge something: fighting for healthcare is exhausting. Every phone call, every form, every appointment, every appeal—it all takes energy. Energy that's already in short supply when you have TBI. Sometimes you won't have the fight in you. Sometimes you'll let things slide because you just can't deal with one more thing.

That's okay. You're not failing. You're surviving. Do what you can, when you can. Rest when you need to. Pick your battles. Get help where you can find it. The system is hard. You're doing your best. •••

For the Caregivers: You Might Be the Fighter If you're a caregiver, here's something important: You might need to be the one who fights. Your loved one's brain is injured. They might not be able to navigate the healthcare system effectively. They might not be able to advocate for themselves. They might not have the energy to push back when they're denied or dismissed. That might fall to you. It's a lot. I know. But patients who have advocates get better care. That's just the reality. If you can help with phone calls, appointments, paperwork, appeals—your help matters more than you know.

Don't Suffer in Silence Let me end this chapter with the most important thing: Don't suffer in silence. Don't assume this is just how it is and nothing can help. Don't give up on getting care because the system is frustrating. Don't isolate yourself because asking for help feels like weakness. There are resources. There are treatments. There are people who can help. You have to look for them. You have to ask. You have to fight sometimes. But they're there. Lean on resources. Try to make friends with other TBI survivors who get it. Join support groups. Find online communities. Connect with people who understand. You don't have to do this alone. The system is bullshit sometimes. But you can still get what you need. It just takes persistence, documentation, and the willingness to keep pushing. Keep pushing.

Before the accident, I knew who I was. Staff Sergeant Joseph Lewis. United States Air Force. EOD technician. Seven years of service. One deployment to Kandahar. I was a husband. I was confident. I was capable. I was the guy who disarmed bombs for a living and didn't flinch. I knew exactly who I was. And then I died in a field in Idaho, and everything changed. •••

The Man Who Died Let me tell you about the man who died that day. He was competent. Skilled. Sure of himself. He had a career, a marriage, a life that made sense. He knew his place in the world. But he also didn't have empathy. Not real empathy. He was closed off. He was hard. He was so busy being confident that he never stopped to consider what other people were going through. He wasn't a bad person. But he wasn't as good as he could have been. That man died in October 2013. He's not coming back. •••

The Man Who Woke Up The man who woke up in that hospital was someone different. Confused. Scared. Childlike. He knew her name but not that she was his wife. Unable to take care of himself. Unable to do any of the things that had defined him before. Everything that had made him "him" was gone—or at least, scrambled beyond recognition. For a long time, that felt like loss. Like failure. Like something had been taken from me that I could never get back. And that's true, in a way. Something was taken. The old me is gone.
But something else happened too. Something I didn't expect. •••

The Great Transformation If I had to give my TBI story a movie title, it would be "The Great Transformation." Because that's what happened. I didn't just survive. I transformed. The things that were taken from me—the confidence, the certainty, the hardness—those weren't all good things. Some of them needed to go. And the things that grew in their place—empathy, compassion, humility, presence—those are better. Genuinely better. I'm not saying TBI is a gift. It's not. It's a brain injury. It sucks. The symptoms suck. The struggle sucks. I would never wish it on anyone. But transformation can happen in the midst of terrible things. Growth can come from pain. You can become someone new—someone better—even when the process of getting there is brutal. That's what happened to me.

Who I Am Now Let me tell you who I am now. I'm a husband—married to the same woman four times, because we kept fighting for each other until we got it right. I'm an artist. I create things. I make music. I explore ideas. The old me didn't have time for that. The new me makes time. I'm a survivor. Not in a dramatic, look-at-me way. Just in the simple way of someone who went through something terrible and is still here. I'm a dude who lived. That's it. Nothing fancy. Just someone who got a second chance and is trying to make something of it. I'm more compassionate than I used to be. More empathetic. More capable of sitting with someone else's pain instead of trying to fix it or dismiss it. I'm humbled. The old me thought he had it all figured out. The new me knows better. I'm present. More than I've ever been. When you almost die, you stop taking moments for granted.

The Friend at the Gate Remember what I told you in the introduction? About my near-death experience? I saw my best friend—the one who died in the motorcycle accident a year before. He was standing at a gate made of light, and he told me I didn't belong there. He said I had a big job to do. And then he pushed me, and I fell back into my body, and I woke up naked in a hospital shower with no idea what had happened. I've thought about that moment a lot over the years. What's the big job? What am I supposed to do? I don't think there's one answer. I don't think there's some specific mission I'm supposed to accomplish and then I'm done. I think the big job is this: becoming who I'm capable of being. Contributing what I can. Helping the people I can help. Maybe writing this book is part of it. Maybe being a better husband is part of it. Maybe just being present for the people around me is part of it.
I don't know exactly what the big job is. But I'm trying to do it. Every day, I'm trying. •••

The Identity Crisis I need to be honest about something: the identity crisis after TBI is real. When everything that defined you is suddenly gone or changed, you don't know who you are anymore. You look in the mirror and see a stranger. You try to do things you used to do and fail. You wonder if there's anything left of the person you were. That's a dark place. I've been there. If you're there right now, I want you to know: it gets better. Not because you go back to who you were— you won't. But because you start to discover who you're becoming. The new identity doesn't come all at once. It builds slowly. You try things. Some work, some don't. You discover new strengths. You accept new limitations. Piece by piece, you assemble a new sense of self. It takes time. It takes patience. It takes the willingness to let go of who you were and embrace who you are.
But it happens. The new you emerges. And they might be pretty great. •••

What I've Learned Let me share what I've learned about identity after TBI: You can't go back. The old you is gone. Spending your energy trying to resurrect them is a waste. Focus forward, not backward. You get to choose who you become. Within the limits of your injury, you have choices. What do you value? What do you want to build? What kind of person do you want to be? You get to decide. Grief is part of it. You're allowed to mourn the person you were. That's not weakness—it's healthy. Grieve them, honor them, and then let them go. Identity is not your abilities. You are not your job title, your skills, your accomplishments. You are something deeper than that. When the external stuff is stripped away, what's left? That's you. The people who love you still love you. You might be different, but you're still lovable. The core of who you are—the soul, the spirit, whatever you want to call it— that's still there. The people who really love you can see it. •••

Advice for the Identity Crisis If you're struggling with who you are after TBI, here's what I'd tell you: Give it time. You're not going to figure this out in a week or a month. Identity rebuilding takes years. Be patient with yourself. Try things. You might discover interests and abilities you didn't have before. The new you might be into things the old you never considered. Experiment. Lean into what you like. What brings you joy? What makes you feel like yourself? Do more of that. Build your new identity around the things that feel right. Talk to other TBI survivors. They get it. They've been through the same identity crisis. Finding your people helps. Consider therapy. A good therapist can help you work through the grief and start building a new sense of self. It's worth it.
Write it down. Journal about who you were, who you are, who you want to be. Putting it on paper helps you see it more clearly. •••

For the People Who Love Us If you love someone going through an identity crisis after TBI, here's what I want you to know: The person you love is still there. They might be different. They might be struggling. But the core of who they are hasn't vanished. Look for it. Connect with it. Don't compare them to before. Every time you say "you used to..." you remind them of what they've lost. Focus on who they are now, not who they were. Support their exploration. They're trying to figure out who they are. Encourage them to try new things. Celebrate their discoveries. Be patient. This process takes time. Years. Don't rush them. Love them through the change. My wife loved the man I was before. She also loves the man I am now. She holds both. That's the kind of love that survives TBI.

You Can't Go Back. But You Can Go Forward. Here's the bottom line: You can't go back to who you were. That person is gone. But you can go forward. You can build something new. You can become someone you never expected to be— and that person might be amazing. Don't give up. Don't stop pushing. Don't assume that because the old you is gone, there's nothing left. There's everything left. You're still here. You're still alive. You still have the capacity to grow, to change, to become. The Great Transformation is possible. I'm living proof. •••
The Big Job My friend pushed me back into this world because he said I had a big job to do. I think part of that big job was writing this book.

If anything I've said here helps you—if it makes you feel less alone, if it gives you strategies that work, if it helps you understand what's happening in your brain— then maybe I've done at least a piece of what I was sent back to do. You have a big job too. I don't know what it is. You might not know what it is yet. But you're here for a reason. You survived for a reason. Find your big job. Do it. Be who you're meant to be. And don't give up. Ever. •••

Final Words If you've made it this far, thank you. Thank you for trusting me with your time. Thank you for letting me share my story. Thank you for being part of this club nobody wanted to join. We're in this together. All of us with our scrambled brains and our broken filters and our emotions that are basically drunk. We're figuring it out. Day by day. One thing at a time. You're not alone. You're never alone. There are millions of us walking this road.

And we're going to be okay. Different than before. Maybe better than before. Definitely stronger than before. Keep going. Keep pushing. Keep building the person you want to be. Because you can't go back to who you used to be. But who you become? That's up to you. •••

sections.h: Caregiver Checklist: What You Need to Know
p: Because the TBI patient will be lost. The caregiver needs instructions. ••• This checklist is for the spouses, parents, children, and friends who are suddenly thrust into the role of caregiver. You didn't ask for this job. You probably have no training for it. But here you are. This is what you need to know. •••

Immediately After Injury ☐ Get everything documented. Every symptom, every diagnosis, every conversation with doctors. Write it down or record it. You will need this later. ☐ Ask questions. Don't assume you understand. Ask the doctors to explain in plain language. Ask again if you need to. ☐ Be present at appointments. Your loved one may not remember what was said. You need to be there to hear it.

☐ Start a medical binder. Keep all paperwork, test results, discharge instructions, medication lists in one place. ☐ Learn the medications. What are they taking? When? What are the side effects? What interactions should you watch for? ☐ Prepare the home. Remove tripping hazards. Create a calm, quiet space. Reduce clutter and chaos. •••

Understanding What's Happening ☐ Learn about TBI. Read about it. Ask doctors to explain it. The more you understand, the better you can help. ☐ Expect personality changes. They may not act like themselves. This is the injury, not a choice. ☐ Expect emotional dysregulation. Anger, tears, mood swings—their emotional thermostat is broken. ☐ Expect memory problems. They will forget things. They will repeat themselves. They will lose things. This is normal. ☐ Expect fatigue. They will need more rest than seems reasonable. Don't push them past their limits.
☐ Expect slow progress. Recovery takes months to years. Don't expect quick fixes. •••

Daily Care ☐ Create routines. Same schedule every day helps their brain cope. ☐ Reduce stimulation. Quiet environments. Dim lights when possible. Limit visitors if needed. ☐ Monitor for overload. Watch for signs they're getting overwhelmed. Help them exit situations before meltdown. ☐ Manage medications. Set up a pill organizer. Set reminders. Don't rely on them to remember. ☐ Assist with hygiene. They may need help with bathing, dressing, grooming—especially early on. ☐ Prepare simple meals. Nutrition matters for brain healing. Make it easy for them to eat well. ☐ Limit decisions. Decision fatigue is real. Make choices for them when you can.

Communication ☐ Speak clearly and simply. Short sentences. One instruction at a time. ☐ Don't rush them. Give them time to process and respond. ☐ Write things down. Important information should be on paper, not just verbal. ☐ Don't finish their sentences. Let them get there themselves, even if it's slow. ☐ Be patient with repetition. They may ask the same question multiple times. Answer calmly each time. ☐ Use signals. Develop non-verbal cues for "slow down," "too loud," "time to leave." •••
Safety ☐ Remove hazards. Loose rugs, sharp corners, clutter they could trip on. ☐ Monitor driving. They probably shouldn't drive, at least for a while. Have the conversation.

☐ Supervise dangerous activities. Cooking, using tools, anything where impaired judgment could cause harm. ☐ Watch for depression. Suicidal thoughts are common after TBI. Take it seriously. Get help. ☐ Know emergency numbers. Doctor, hospital, crisis line—have them ready. •••

Taking Care of Yourself ☐ You matter too. Your needs are not less important just because they're injured. ☐ Get support. Find a support group for caregivers. Talk to a therapist. Lean on friends and family. ☐ Take breaks. You cannot pour from an empty cup. Schedule time for yourself. ☐ Accept help. When people offer, say yes. Let them bring meals, sit with your loved one, run errands. ☐ Watch for burnout. Exhaustion, resentment, hopelessness—these are signs you need more support. ☐ Don't feel guilty. Having mixed emotions is normal. Being frustrated doesn't mean you don't love them.

Long-Term ☐ Understand this is a marathon. Recovery takes years. Pace yourself accordingly. ☐ Celebrate small wins. Progress might be slow, but it's still progress. Notice it. Acknowledge it. ☐ Adjust expectations. They may not return to who they were. Learn to love who they're becoming. ☐ Keep documenting. For disability claims, for medical records, for your own reference. ☐ Revisit the care plan. As they change, their needs change. Reassess regularly. ☐ Plan for the future. Financial planning, legal planning, long-term care considerations. •••
